00-start-here/canon-policy.title: Canon Policy
00-start-here/canon-policy.content:
Canon Policy
One-Line Summary
The vault supports exploratory lore, but only reviewed and approved material should become production-facing canon.
Canon Levels

hard-canon: true unless explicitly revised.
soft-canon: currently accepted but open to revision.
in-world-belief: believed by a faction, culture, or character; may be false.
rumor: unreliable, mythic, propaganda, or contradictory.
reference: external inspiration or trope study; not canon.
rejected: explicitly not part of Neon Champions.
game-bridge: design translation from lore into playable systems.

Status Levels

seed: rough idea.
draft: coherent but not reviewed.
reviewed: discussed and internally consistent.
approved: accepted as production-facing canon or design guidance.
deprecated: superseded, preserved for history.

Approval Rule
The agent may draft, organize, research, cross-link, and identify contradictions.
The user owns canon approval.
No major world rule, faction identity, or production-facing lore should be promoted to approved without explicit user approval.
Contradiction Rule
Contradictions are not automatically bad. They may represent:

faction propaganda
mythic uncertainty
unreliable witnesses
incomplete science
old draft residue
genuine canon conflict

Useful contradictions should be documented. Harmful contradictions should be resolved.
Mirror Rule
Only mirror material to a game repo when:

it is approved or explicitly selected by the user;
it has game_relevance: medium, high, or core;
it has a design bridge or production-facing summary.

00-start-here/champions-documentation-au.title: Champions Documentation Audit — 2026-07-13
00-start-here/champions-documentation-au.content:
Champions Documentation Audit — 2026-07-13
Scope
Compared available Hermes session history with the current world vault and game-design repository to determine whether major Champion decisions remain chat-only.
Key history windows checked:

2026-05-15: initial Champion ontology, social ambiguity, faction-relative recognition, Cyberpunk-style legends, transhumanist/strong-leader myth, and parasocial worship.
2026-05-18: Champions as a human-exceptionalist answer to AI anxiety.
2026-05-22: Champions as public faces, deniable operators, strategic hero-commanders, and users of Intel-upgraded Assets.
2026-05-28 onward: off-board commander assumption; Marshal/Operator poles; Command, Operations, Doctrine, primary stats, progression, recruitment, defeat, Assets, and secondary skills.
2026-07-10: Claude’s July 6 plan containing faction-specific Champion seeds for HRC, QXZ, Barents, and an obsolete war-OS version of Janus-Kestrel.
2026-07-13: Champions as the coalition gravity that can make a loose HRC protection network operate as one faction.

Verdict
CONCERNS — mostly recorded, but fragmented
The major Champion ideas were not lost. The current documents preserve substantially more than the chat-level summaries alone suggest. The problem is fragmentation and authority clarity rather than missing bulk content.
Well Covered
World ontology and social meaning
canon/world-rules/champions.md records:

Championhood as partly condition, role, title, reputation, recognition, and myth;
no universal biological definition or required superpower;
faction-relative, popular, battlefield, technological, self-claimed, and refused recognition;
corporate assets, legends, commanders, rebels, saints, frauds, and ordinary people elevated through deeds;
transhumanist/übermensch and strong-leader mythology;
social love, fear, loathing, exploitation, envy, and worship;
possible origin in human-exceptionalist reaction to AI displacement.

cultures/champion-worship.md records the parasocial, celebrity, religious, political, and Chorus-mediated layer.
Game-facing role
design-bridges/champions-design-bridge.md records:

Champions as HoMM-style strategic hero-commanders rather than generic superheroes;
army, faction, territory, reputation, body modification, and story integration;
recognition tiers, false/failed/illegal/refused Champions;
progression, dependency, Assets, resource hooks, faction signaling, and campaign consequences.

Detailed systems
The game-design GDD design/gdd/tactical-combat/champion-operations-and-progression.md records approved or working decisions for:

off-board command role;
Marshal/Operator archetype poles;
Command, Operations, and Doctrine;
primary stats and progression;
Operation channels, preparation, resistance, and counterplay;
Champion build grammar and unit specialization;
curated/rotating faction and neutral recruitment;
HoMM-like defeat as loss of control rather than routine permanent death;
personal and command-layer Assets;
Intel upgrades and duplicate dismantling;
secondary skill pool, ranks, offer rules, and starting skills.

Gaps Found and Repaired
1. Why factions cohere around Champions
The documents listed many reasons troops might follow Champions, but did not clearly state that unstable factions can form around them rather than merely employ them.
Repair: added Faction Gravity and Command to canon/world-rules/champions.md. It preserves multiple command mechanisms and records HRC as the first explicit case of Champion-mediated coalition formation.
2. HRC-specific Champion relationship
The former HRC page treated Champions as an open question and described the coalition more like a stable local faction.
Repair: revised organizations/home-rule-coalition.md so the pre-crisis network exists without unified command, while different Champions pull different institutions, activists, workers, volunteers, and defectors into temporary operational coalitions.
3. Discovery and source hierarchy
World ontology, cultural meaning, design bridge, and detailed mechanics live in separate artifacts without a single status map.
Current reading order:

canon/world-rules/champions.md — what Championhood means in-world; soft-canon seed.
cultures/champion-worship.md — public myth and parasocial culture; soft-canon seed.
design-bridges/champions-design-bridge.md — translation into strategic hero/commander functions; game bridge.
Game-design design/gdd/tactical-combat/champion-operations-and-progression.md — detailed system decisions and working contracts.

4. Named candidate discovery
The first pass correctly found the system and ontology material but missed faction-specific seeds embedded inside the long Claude plan pasted on 2026-07-10. Those concepts were not present in current named-character authority.
Repair: recovered and preserved them without canon promotion in raw/brainstorms/claude-champion-seeds-2026-07-06.md. The note separates reusable character cores from rejected Protocol terminology, obsolete faction roles, and protagonist/antagonist framing.
Important Unresolved Questions
These should remain open rather than being silently inferred from mechanics:

Is every player-controlled hero a Champion, or can ordinary officers command armies?
How many Champions can a faction field, recognize, or sustain at once?
Which parts of Champion distinction are materially measurable, and which exist only through recognition?
How much personal battlefield presence should individual Champions have outside the current off-board tactical baseline?
What is the first campaign’s named HRC Champion, and which coalition currents recognize them?
How does QXZ manufacture, sponsor, insure, audit, or legally own its Champions?
Which Champion mechanics are prototype commitments versus later product scope?

Conclusion
No wholesale Champion rewrite is needed. The central ontology, social myth, strategic role, and detailed mechanical vocabulary are already documented. Future work should focus on named Champions, faction-specific relationships, player-facing clarity, and resolving a few high-level authority questions—not recreating the system from memory.

00-start-here/open-questions.title: Open Questions
00-start-here/open-questions.content:
Open Questions
Purpose
This page tracks unresolved worldbuilding questions for Neon Champions.
Questions can be resolved into canon pages, mystery pages, rejected ideas, trope studies, or design bridges.
Foundational Questions

Is 2052 the default present year, or should the setting sit earlier/later within the 2048-2058 range?
What exactly is a Champion?
Did the Champion category begin as a humanist answer to AI replacement, before becoming muddled and captured by other entities?
Which mix of competence, recognition, system access, charisma, logistics, legal authority, and coalition-building makes each faction’s Champions strategically decisive?
What is the Digital-Net: network, territory, ecology, ghost layer, AI habitat, infrastructure, or all of these?
What does the Digital-Net want, if anything?
What is mutation in this world: disease, upgrade path, weapon, ecology, spiritualized identity, or class marker?
What prevents this world from using direct magic?
What event or process created the current world order?
Is there truly no AGI in this world, or is AGI hidden, misclassified, distributed, or politically denied?
What specific AI scare, blackout, war, hoax, or near-miss created the current compute/energy regime?
Did the AGI Compact begin before the UNP, or was it one of the UNP Charter’s founding bargains?
What exact threshold separates legal virtual intelligence from forbidden AGI/ASI: compute, capability, autonomy, self-improvement, legal personhood, or some negotiated combination?
Which recognized Great Corporate Person is most suspected of hiding a forbidden model or threshold-crossing research program?
When was the White Sky deployed, and was it sudden, gradual, regional, covert, or openly emergency-driven?
Which regions benefited from the White Sky, which were sacrificed, and who controls albedo tuning now?
How did the White Sky reshape solar energy, cooling, compute sovereignty, migration rights, and body-subscription dependency?
Which American, Chinese, Singaporean, Swiss-routed, insurer, sovereign-wealth, or private-family interests actually benefit from QXZ Meridian?
Which Swiss, Luxembourgish, Singaporean, Nordic, Gulf, Pacific, or semiconductor interests actually benefit from Helvetia and its lawful-cognition custody regime?
Was the first deployment publicly announced as emergency rescue, hidden as a field trial, or denied until measurable cooling made it politically irreversible?
Where are the major Meridian Stations, who guards them, and which states or movements contest them?
Which named cities, regions, corporations, clinics, fleets, and factions make the current world concrete rather than abstract?

Social / Political Questions

Who owns body modification?
Who controls memory, identity, and resurrection technologies?
How does Helvetia ration compute, energy access, model licensing, and AI service tiers without becoming a de facto world government?
Are corporations still dominant, or have they become city-states, cults, or quasi-governments?
Is United Nations and Persons the formal charter name, or a common shorthand for a longer post-UN institution?
Which state blocs accepted corporate seats in the UNP reluctantly, and which still reject the arrangement as corporate feudalism?
Are the Great Corporate Persons exactly nine by charter, or is nine only the current recognized count after Chorus Exchange was admitted?
Can non-corporate persons — labor federations, city compacts, indigenous authorities, universities, or Echo estates — receive UNP standing?
What does everyday life look like for non-Champions?
What does social status mean in a body-hacked, surveillance-saturated world?

Game-Bridge Questions

Which lore elements should map directly to faction asymmetry?
Which world resources create strategic pressure?
What replaces fantasy mines, mana, artifacts, and spells in this world?
Can compute and energy infrastructure replace or supplement fantasy mines/mana as strategic map resources?
What makes map exploration feel dangerous and wondrous?
What kinds of heroes/commanders does this world produce?

Related Pages

worldbuilding-charter
canon-policy
virtual-intelligence-and-compute-scarcity
qxz-meridian
timeline-and-social-pressure-points
white-sky
worldbuilding-development-audit

World Map / Political Economy Questions

Should the world map be presented primarily through nations, blocs, corporate regions, maintenance/sacrifice/contest zones, or a layered UI that shows all of them?
Which exact high-asset regions benefited most from the white-sky and therefore defend it sincerely: North Atlantic insurance/finance states, Pacific manufacturing corridors, Gulf/desert engineering states, or protected food-logistics regions?
Should West Africa/Sahel/Gulf of Guinea be the main visibly harmed white-sky opposition region, with conflict centered on monsoon timing, rainfall attribution, flood risk, solar-curtailment claims, and climate-for-concessions deals?
Are corporate regions normalized worldwide, or concentrated in former/debt-distressed developmental economies plus disaster-hit rich cities?
Which corporate-region archetype is most central to the player-facing setting: climate migration work-towns, debt-receivership cities, critical mineral/infrastructure concessions, biosecure health zones, port/cable corridors, or bonded cloud/compute concessions?
Should a campaign-era crisis be the Blue Week, a monsoon-theft tribunal, a cable famine, a limb-repo uprising, or a receivership coup?
From world-map-political-economy-recommendations-2026-05-20, which synthesis should be promoted first into canon-facing pages: corporate concessions, West African rainfall claimants, compute freeports, migration work-towns, or a world-map design bridge?
From nation-states-and-real-world-continuity-2052, which current countries must remain especially recognizable for player orientation, and which, if any, should have formally changed borders or sovereignty status?
Should the next canon-facing map page be state-continuity-and-layered-sovereignty, clarifying that countries still exist while corporate/climate labels are overlays?
From europe-nato-russia-china-japan-cyberpunk-2052, should the default be: EU survives as a climate-liability union, NATO survives as a continuity alliance, Russia survives as a militarized uneven federation, China is a rival/co-architect of White Sky, and Japan remains influential through disaster adaptation, robotics, body dignity, and feed authenticity?

Baltic War / Eastern Europe Questions

From baltic-war, what exact year should the Baltic War begin, and how long should the Vistula-Daugava phase last?
What is the formal legal relationship between NATO, the EU, the European Security Compact, and European Strategic Command after the Treaty of Tallinn?
Is Vezha Systems independent, state-protected, partially employee/veteran-owned, or already captured by European finance?
Did Vezha Systems remain Ukrainian-controlled, become European-financed, or become a contested state-corporate platform after the war?
What exact charter governs Kantograd: European Security Compact, UN-like trusteeship, Russian residual sovereignty, or bespoke free-city treaty?
What is the final status of Belarus’s neutral zone: sovereign neutral state, supervised buffer, federation, or frozen gray zone?
Does Chechnya become formally independent, functionally independent, or the center of a broader Caucasian sovereignty rupture?
Which Champions, veterans, or Echo cases from the Baltic War become player-visible myths?
Which company, public program, charity, or military archive created the first widely adopted Memorial Echoes for families of the war dead?
When did Echoes cross the line from grief prosthetics into legally or militarily meaningful continuity shells?

UNP / AGI Compact / Megacorp Order Questions

After accepting the  AGI Compact formula, what founding trauma made the arrangement politically unavoidable?
Should the UNP’s core crisis body be called the Continuity Council, or does that sound too on-the-nose?
Which powers sit on the Continuity Council: states, regional blocs, Great Corporate Persons, rotating regions, labor/city/person chambers, or technical inspectorates?
Should Axiom become the accepted fifth Great Corporate Person for identity, civil registry, feed provenance, evidence, and Echo recognition?
Which three remaining continuity layers should fill the megacorp roster after qxz-meridian, Vezha Systems, barents-research-group, helvetia, and the possible Axiom: body, food, ports/cables/orbit, or something else?
What exact AGI-threshold scare, leaked model, illegal training run, or compute blackmail incident made Helvetia politically unavoidable?
What was the founding trauma that made the UNP politically possible: White Sky first move, AGI near-miss, Baltic War escalation, cable famine, food shock, or a chained crisis?
What types of war remain common despite the charter: concession wars, model-freeport raids, private-security campaigns, proxy labs, feed-provenance conflicts, registry sabotage, or Champion operations?
What founding trauma made Axiom politically unavoidable: deepfake election crisis, registry cyberwar, climate-displacement identity loss, land-title fraud cascade, Echo inheritance scandal, or the Axiom-SOVRAN merger crisis?

Arctic / Polar Megacorp Questions

Is Barents Research Group still formally headquartered in a Nordic jurisdiction, or has it become a treaty-layered holding structure?
Does BRG operate under public scientific charters, private concession law, or Arctic emergency authority?
Are there Bering / Pacific-Arctic rivals, or is BRG already global across the whole polar frontier?
Which indigenous, local, state, or activist groups most visibly oppose BRG?
Does BRG control White Sky calibration infrastructure directly, or only the polar data that others depend on?

Food and Nutrient Continuity
The next Great Corporate Person candidate is now Verdant, a food / nutrient / seed / famine logistics megacorp controlling seed traits, fertilizer, crop insurance, grain routing, emergency rations, fermentation protein, and urban nutrient recovery.
Accepted naming direction:

Verdant — ordinary public name.
Verdant Covenant Group — likely formal/treaty style.
Feed the World Initiative — sinister humanitarian/public-good interface.
Common Table Systems — deprecated as too strange/soft.

Key risk: avoid making it just “Monsanto but bigger.” Its power should be the operating conditions of food continuity: seed, nutrients, credit, insurance, routing, rations, relief thresholds, and nutrient loops.
Body Continuity Candidate
Should the seventh Great Corporate Person candidate be Vitae Continuity, a body-continuity megacorp controlling organs, prosthetics, fertility, chronic care, veteran repair, occupational viability, and biological uptime?
Leading direction:

Vitae Continuity — strongest current recommendation; broad, plausible, and institution-scale.
Continuance Health Combine — darker and more industrial; useful if the parent should feel more brutal.
SomaDyne Continuity Group — stronger prosthetic/body-engineering flavor; likely better as a subsidiary.

Boundary to preserve: QXZ Meridian owns climate exposure and adaptation finance; Vitae owns biological repair and functional uptime after exposure reaches the body.
Threshold Logistics Candidate
Should the eighth Great Corporate Person candidate be Janus-Kestrel Continuity Group, a threshold-logistics and signal-circulation megacorp controlling ports, customs, cargo identity, cable landings, drone corridors, orbital relays, bonded corridors, emergency exception status, and lawful movement?
Leading direction:

Janus-Kestrel Continuity Group — current strongest recommendation; Janus gives gates, thresholds, customs, and exception law, while Kestrel adds drones, couriers, relays, speed, and aerial/orbital movement.
Gatehouse Continuity Authority — drier, more bureaucratic alternative if Janus feels too mythic.
BlueGate Continuity Group — more humanitarian/sea-sky-network alternative.

Boundary to preserve: Barents Research Group certifies polar frontiers; Janus controls circulation through global thresholds.
Strong challenger: a media/communications/finance Great Person such as Chorus Exchange, controlling attention, payments, remittances, creator income, subscription bundles, and everyday liquidity. Energy/grid remains important but probably below Great Person rank for now; Nadir Gridworks is a strong name for an independent mid-major or continuity contractor handling blackstart grids, district cooling, port backup power, and receiver-city energy concessions.
Media-Finance and Nadir Candidates
From janus-kestrel-media-finance-nadir-2026-05-22, the media/communications/banking megacorp is now accepted as the ninth Great Corporate Person.
Accepted direction:

Chorus Exchange — attention and liquidity continuity: feeds, creator income, remittances, payroll rails, ad markets, subscriptions, payment identity, microcredit, consumer financial reach, and Champion-public monetization.

Boundary to preserve:

Axiom authenticates truth and identity.
Helvetia controls lawful cognition and model custody.
Janus-Kestrel carries signals and goods through hard infrastructure.
Chorus amplifies, monetizes, and settles everyday social-financial life.

How openly should Chorus Exchange sponsor or manufacture Champions, rather than merely monetizing every faction’s Champions?
Where should Nadir Gridworks sit?
Current best answer: not a Great Person yet; use it as an independent mid-major / recognized continuity contractor for blackstart power, district microgrids, cooling basements, port backup systems, and receiver-city energy concessions.

00-start-here/worldbuilding-charter.title: Worldbuilding Charter
00-start-here/worldbuilding-charter.content:
Worldbuilding Charter
One-Line Summary
Neon Champions is a cyberpunk/biopunk strategy-RPG world where White Sky climate trauma, energy and compute sovereignty, subscription bodies, polluted synthetic reality, mutation, VI restraint, and the Digital-Net produce Champions who feel mythic without using direct magic.
Purpose
This charter defines the creative boundaries for Neon Champions worldbuilding.
The worldbuilding vault exists to explore lore deeply, not only to serve immediate gameplay. However, stable lore should eventually support faction identity, strategic map design, heroes, units, campaigns, resources, progression, and player fantasy.
Current Anchors

Cyberpunk turn-based strategy/RPG energy.
Inspired partly by Heroes of Might and Magic 3’s strategic pressure, factions, maps, and power growth.
No direct magic.
Strange biotech, mutation, rogue AI, and Digital-Net phenomena can create effects that feel supernatural in-world.
Single-player is primary; multiplayer options may exist.

Draft World Pillars
These are provisional and should be stress-tested.

Power always has a source, cost, and contamination.
The Digital-Net is infrastructure, battlefield, afterlife, and disease vector.
Champions are political weapons, cultural icons, and unstable anomalies.
Factions express incompatible philosophies of human evolution.
The White Sky is a literal climate wound before it is a metaphor: a visible planetary intervention that reshapes equality, energy, compute, bodies, feeds, and territory.
Synthetic reality is useful but polluted; free-net access exists, but it is uneven, dangerous, and never pure.
Public machine rule is taboo. VI influence should be deniable, bureaucratic, and laundered through scores, dashboards, protocols, and advisory systems rather than open AI sovereignty.

Draft Anti-Pillars

No direct spellcasting or ungrounded magic systems.
No generic cyberpunk megacity with shallow neon aesthetics only.
No lore that makes factions mechanically or culturally interchangeable.
No clean utopian transhumanism without social, bodily, or identity costs.
No omniscient single truth when competing myths, propaganda, and partial explanations are stronger.

Open Charter Questions

What exactly is a Champion in-world?
What does the Digital-Net want, if anything?
Was there a single core catastrophe or a slow cascade?
How public, commercialized, or feared is mutation?
Are Champions rare individuals, manufactured assets, elected icons, infected hosts, or all of these depending on faction?
Which factions defend, reverse, regionalize, privatize, or sabotage the White Sky?
How much of Echo identity is real continuity versus grief product, model imitation, or legal fiction?

00-start-here/worldbuilding-development-.title: Worldbuilding Development Audit

00-start-here/worldbuilding-review-and-d.title: Worldbuilding Review and Design-Readiness Plan
00-start-here/worldbuilding-review-and-d.content:
Worldbuilding Review and Design-Readiness Plan
Purpose
This review captures the current state of the Neon Champions wiki after the May 2026 expansion, identifies the most interesting material, names the loose connections, and proposes the next design-ready development pass.
It is a planning/audit page, not canon.
What Is Strong and Interesting
1. Maintenance as power
The strongest setting engine is that civilization survives through systems it cannot safely turn off: white-sky, agi-compact-and-compute-deterrence, great-corporate-persons, biotech-and-mutation, synthetic-reality-and-polluted-feeds, echo-identity-and-death, and world-map-and-political-economy.
This is better than generic megacorp dystopia. The horror is dependency, liability, auditability, uptime, and continuity.
2. White Sky is a literal and political image
white-sky works because it is visible before it is metaphorical. Everyone lives under the same altered sky, but not everyone receives the same safety, cooling, insurance, rainfall, clean feed, or adaptation body.
The best extensions are not more climate theory. They are concrete: Meridian Stations, deployment geography, maintenance rituals, sacrificial regions, blue-sky breaks, and everyday sky politics.
3. The Great Corporate Persons have a distinct organizing principle
The current roster is compelling because each entity controls a continuity layer rather than a product category:













































LayerCurrent directionAtmosphere / climate exposureqxz-meridianWar OS / city resilienceVezha SystemsPolar routes / extraction / databarents-research-groupFrontier compute / lawful cognitionhelvetiaIdentity / admissible realityaxiomFood / nutrient continuityverdantBody continuityVitae Continuity, currently in megacorp-7-body-continuity-2026-05-22Threshold logistics / ports / cables / orbitJanus-Kestrel, currently in megacorp-8-threshold-logistics-2026-05-22 and janus-kestrel-media-finance-nadir-2026-05-22Attention / liquidity / reputationchorus-exchange
This gives the world strategic sponsors without making every faction a corporation.
4. Baltic War → Echoes → Vezha is emotionally grounded
The baltic-war now does useful work: it explains European security trauma, Ukrainian doctrine, Vezha Systems, kantograd, and the origin of Memorial Echoes.
Echoes are strongest when they begin as grief technology, not as a clean immortality product.
5. Champions have strong social charge
champions and champion-worship connect transhuman bodies, AI anxiety, celebrity, myth, strong-leader politics, and strategic command. chorus-exchange gives Champion fame real infrastructure.
The risk is that Champion still means too many things.
Main Gaps
1. Design bridges are missing
The wiki has lore pages and raw brainstorms, but almost no actual design-bridges/ pages. The first bridge set should be:

design-bridges/champions.md
design-bridges/white-sky-and-meridian-stations.md
design-bridges/digital-net-and-polluted-feed.md
design-bridges/body-subscriptions-and-mutation.md
design-bridges/great-corporate-persons.md
design-bridges/world-map-and-campaign-crisis.md

2. Factions are still axes, not factions
factions-as-evolutionary-philosophies is useful, but the wiki needs actual faction seed pages. The first six should probably be:

Sky Loyalists / Stabilization Citizens
Blue Restorationists / Open Sky cells
Body Sovereigns
Free-Net Archivists
Human-Exceptionalist Champion Leagues
Machine-Emergence / VI-Acceleration sects

Each faction needs worldview, territory/power base, body philosophy, Digital-Net posture, Champion posture, heroic version, horrific version, visuals, and strategic hooks.
3. Champions need boundaries
Needed constraints:

who can certify or deny Champion status;
rarity by region;
difference between celebrity, elite operator, altered person, and Champion;
required costs and maintenance;
false / failed / illegal / retired / Echo Champions;
why armies and publics follow Champions despite drones, VI, and professional officers.

4. Digital-Net needs architecture
digital-net is a central mystery but not yet a concrete network. It needs layers:

public feed layer;
corporate service layer;
municipal sensor layer;
battlefield mesh;
Axiom-certified record layer;
Chorus attention/payment layer;
Helvetia lawful-compute layer;
Free-Net fragments;
dead archives;
Echo-contaminated zones;
hostile model farms.

Each layer should have access methods, dangers, class markers, typical users, and game hooks.
5. Everyday life is thin
The setting has strong macro institutions but needs lived texture:

commute under polluted overlays;
cheap blue-sky subscriptions;
body-plan downgrades;
clinic waiting rooms;
Echo mourning;
food-continuity ration thresholds;
Champion fan economies;
Axiom proof rituals;
Chorus greylisting;
Free-Net archive raids.

6. Timeline spine is not yet settled
The wiki needs a single timeline that aligns:

Baltic War / Vistula-Daugava War;
Memorial Echo origins;
White Sky deployment;
UNP formation;
AGI Compact formalization;
Great Corporate Person recognition;
Blue Week.

Without this, the setting is coherent thematically but slightly floating historically.
Loose Connections to Tie Together
White Sky + Chorus
Chorus should not only monetize Champions. It should monetize sky perception: blue-sky overlays, climate dashboards, verified outrage, disaster streams, restoration martyrdom, and Sky Loyalist reassurance.
Axiom + Echoes + AGI Compact
Axiom decides identity/admissibility; Helvetia decides lawful cognition; Echoes sit at the boundary. A dedicated page should explain why advanced Echoes are not automatically forbidden AGI, or why some factions think they are.
Verdant + Janus-Kestrel + World Map
Food may exist but fail to arrive or fail to become administratively recognized as famine. Verdant controls feedability; Janus-Kestrel controls movement; Axiom controls records; Chorus controls attention. This is a strong campaign-crisis machine.
Vezha + Champions
Vezha’s war-OS doctrine can explain why Champions matter militarily: some Champions may be human command/legitimacy/coordination nodes who can operate inside degraded, jammed, politically constrained battlefields where pure VI command is illegal or distrusted.
Blue Week + Factions
blue-week should create at least three faction myths: proof the sky can return, proof sabotage can kill, and proof QXZ/Axiom/Chorus can hide or distort planetary truth.
Contradictions / Tensions to Resolve or Preserve

QXZ overlaps with Verdant and future Vitae. Boundary: QXZ owns exposure and adaptation eligibility; Verdant owns food continuity; Vitae owns biological uptime.
Great Corporate Persons currently mix accepted seats and candidates. Clean roster needed after Vitae and Janus-Kestrel are promoted.
“The Eight” remains as an alias even though the roster is now nine. Decide whether it is deprecated, historical, or public shorthand.
Blue-sky breaks need physical rules: regional thinning, aerosol collapse, feed correction, counter-chemistry, or sabotage.
Echoes need a legal boundary under the AGI Compact.

Recommended Development Order
Phase 1: Wiki and publication hygiene

Publish all current material, including raw/brainstorms/ and raw/references/.
Fix public Quartz base URL to myriwe-bot.github.io/neon-champions-world-site.
Keep index/log/schema current.
Run link/tag/page-count checks after publication.

Phase 2: Promote missing megacorp seats

Create organizations/vitae.md.
Create organizations/janus-kestrel.md.
Rewrite great-corporate-persons into a clean nine-seat roster table.
Update united-nations-and-persons to reference all nine.

Phase 3: Build the playable faction layer
Create the first six faction seed pages listed above. Do not make them final rosters yet; make them strong philosophies with concrete rituals, places, dependencies, and contradictions.
Phase 4: Make Champions design-legible

Rewrite champions with constraints, types, costs, certification, failure modes, and examples.
Expand champion-worship into subcultures.
Create design-bridges/champions.md.

Phase 5: Add core design bridges
Create the six design bridge pages listed in Main Gaps. These are the bridge from lore wiki to game design/GDD.
Phase 6: Add timeline and everyday life

Create canon/timeline/setting-timeline.md.
Create cultures/everyday-life-under-white-sky.md.
Add a handful of short in-world scenes: clinic, feed, commute, food queue, Echo mourning, Champion event.

Superpowers Gate Questions
Use these to decide the next implementation/design plan. Answer one at a time, starting with the first.


Should the next pass prioritize design-readiness or lore concreteness?

A: Design-readiness: create design bridges first.
B: Lore concreteness: factions, everyday life, and timeline first.
C: Megacorp completion: Vitae, Janus-Kestrel, and roster cleanup first.



Should the Great Corporate Person roster now be treated as exactly nine, or as the current nine with future political churn?


Should raw brainstorm and reference pages remain publicly published by default? Current direction from this task: yes.


What should Champions primarily become for design purposes?

hero/commander units;
faction leaders;
strategic propaganda assets;
rare map entities;
all of the above with strict constraints.



Which first faction should be developed deeply enough to become a playable prototype reference?

SCHEMA.title: SCHEMA
SCHEMA.content:
Neon Champions Worldbuilding Wiki Schema
Domain
This Obsidian vault describes the lore, setting, world rules, factions, technologies, histories, myths, conflicts, mysteries, and player-facing worldbuilding of Neon Champions.
It supports two goals:

Lore depth: build a coherent, strange, compelling world that exists beyond immediate gameplay needs.
Game bridge: selectively translate lore into factions, units, maps, campaign structure, mechanics, UI language, and player fantasy.

The vault must preserve creative ambiguity without letting the setting become incoherent.
Operating Model
The vault is the living world. It may contain drafts, myths, contradictions, rejected ideas, and trope experiments.
The future game-repo mirror under design/world/ should contain only approved or stable production-facing lore and design bridges.
Canon, world-rule, technology, faction, culture, location, character, organization, conflict, and mystery pages should primarily read as in-universe setting material. They may use frontmatter for canon/status metadata, but the body should avoid real-world research citations, agent instructions, and design notes unless those are clearly separated.
Use this separation:

raw/references/ for real-world research notes and source summaries.
trope-studies/ for out-of-universe pattern analysis.
design-bridges/ for gameplay/mechanics translation.
00-start-here/ audit or planning pages for agent-facing rewrite notes.
canon/lore pages for what is true, believed, seen, argued, feared, bought, enforced, or mythologized inside the world.

If a canon page starts accumulating broad neighboring concepts, split or link them rather than letting the page become a general setting essay.
Canon Levels
Every non-raw page must declare one canon level:

hard-canon: true unless explicitly revised.
soft-canon: currently accepted but open to revision.
in-world-belief: believed by a faction, culture, or character; may be false.
rumor: unreliable, mythic, propaganda, or contradictory.
reference: external inspiration or trope study; not canon.
rejected: explicitly not part of Neon Champions.
game-bridge: design translation from lore into playable systems.

Status Levels
Every non-raw page must declare one status:

seed: rough idea.
draft: coherent but not reviewed.
reviewed: discussed and internally consistent.
approved: accepted as production-facing canon or design guidance.
deprecated: superseded, preserved for history.

Page Types
Valid page types:

canon/history/baltic-war.title: The Baltic War
canon/history/baltic-war.content:
The Baltic War
One-Line Summary
The Baltic War — later formalized in many histories as the Vistula-Daugava War — was the early-2030s conflict in which Russia’s attempt to force a northeastern European fait accompli instead created the European Security Compact, restored Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders, and turned Ukrainian wartime know-how into a global strategic industry.
Canon Status
Soft canon, reviewed direction. Core outcomes are currently treated as strong setting assumptions:

Ukraine exits the war with its full internationally recognized borders, including Crimea and Sevastopol.
NATO survives only as a diminished or mutated legacy framework; Europe creates a faster parallel security architecture.
Ukraine is not rescued passively. It is the southern powerhouse whose doctrine and defense technology hard-carry the war.
Russia survives, but damaged and constrained.
Belarus becomes a neutral zone.
Kaliningrad is reconstituted as Kantograd, a free city.

Background
By the late 2020s, the Russo-Ukrainian war had hardened into a frozen or semi-frozen conflict. The front no longer consumed the world’s attention every hour, but it had not produced a legitimate settlement. Ukraine remained armed, mobilized, technically inventive, and legally committed to the restoration of all occupied territory.
NATO still existed, but its credibility had thinned. The alliance was not dead on paper. It was weakened by procedural delay, domestic polarization, veto politics, US distraction, legal ambiguity around cyber and hybrid attacks, and years of underestimating how quickly a border crisis could become a continental survival test.
Russia’s leadership misread this weakness. It assumed that Europe would debate, Washington would hesitate, and a limited seizure on the Baltic frontier could be frozen into another territorial “fact.”
What Happened
Russia opened the crisis with pressure against the Baltic frontier: cyberattacks, grid disruption, rail sabotage, drone strikes, naval threats, disinformation, and limited ground actions around the northeastern flank. The early war centered on Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Belarusian launch corridors, and the Kaliningrad axis.
The first phase was frightening. NATO’s formal response moved too slowly. European governments argued over thresholds, attribution, escalation, and American timing. This delay became known in later political memory as the Article Five Failure.
The response that mattered came through emergency European coordination. The Treaty of Tallinn created the European Security Compact and an integrated European Strategic Command. What began as a temporary wartime mechanism became the permanent security spine of post-NATO Europe.
Ukraine entered the war as the southern powerhouse. Its commanders, drone engineers, battlefield software companies, electronic-warfare units, artillery integration teams, civil-defense planners, and repair networks supplied the methods Europe lacked. Europe supplied mass: factories, satellites, money, transport, air defense, legal cover, logistics, and industrial replacement capacity.
The war was won when European scale met Ukrainian doctrine.
Why Russia Lost
Russia could destroy, disrupt, and terrorize. It could not sustain maneuver against an integrated European-Ukrainian system.
Its weaknesses were exposed:

rail-dependent logistics;
brittle command structures;
corruption in procurement and readiness;
visible supply chains under sensor saturation;
exhausted officer culture;
overconfidence in cyber and disinformation effects;
failure to understand how far Ukrainian drone doctrine had advanced.

The European-Ukrainian coalition did not defeat Russia because it was morally pure or frictionless. It defeated Russia because the coalition eventually made the battlefield legible, networked, redundant, and too expensive for Russia to continue.
Ukraine’s Role
Ukraine became the war’s decisive military culture.
The late-2020s frozen conflict had made Ukraine a laboratory of modern war: cheap drones, counter-drone systems, artillery networking, repair improvisation, battlefield software, civil resilience, feed verification, electronic camouflage, and decentralized command.
During the Baltic War, that knowledge scaled across Europe. Ukrainian officers trained European units. Ukrainian software fused sensor feeds. Ukrainian companies supplied drone command layers, logistics platforms, target validation systems, electronic-warfare hygiene, and casualty-routing tools. Ukrainian civil-defense habits became European doctrine almost overnight.
The postwar myth says Europe saved Ukraine and the Baltics. The harsher military truth says Ukraine taught Europe how not to die.
The Restoration of Ukraine
The final settlement restored Ukraine’s full internationally recognized borders, including Crimea and Sevastopol. This became one of the foundation stones of the postwar order.
The slogan was legalistic but powerful:

Occupation can exist. It cannot mature into law.

For Europe, Ukrainian territorial integrity became more than solidarity. It became the legal proof that the new security system had meaning. For Ukraine, restoration did not bring innocence or peace. It brought reconstruction, militarized prestige, defense-industrial power, veteran politics, and a permanent place near the center of European strategy.
Course of the War
The Baltic War is usually taught as three overlapping phases rather than one clean campaign.
Phase One: The Fait Accompli Gamble
Russia’s initial assumption was that Europe would hesitate long enough for geography to become politics. Moscow expected several days or weeks of attribution disputes, NATO procedural paralysis, and arguments over whether cyberattacks, “local protection operations,” and drone strikes crossed the formal threshold for continental war.
The opening moves therefore favored ambiguity:

pressure around Narva and northeastern Estonia;
threats to the Suwałki corridor between Poland and Lithuania;
Belarusian launch corridors and rail pressure;
Kaliningrad-based intimidation in the Baltic Sea;
grid, port, rail, satellite, feed, and insurance-market attacks;
claims of protecting Russian-speaking populations;
synthetic footage and model-poisoning designed to slow political consensus.

Russia did not plan to occupy all of Europe. It planned to break confidence, take limited ground, and freeze the result.
Phase Two: The Article Five Failure
The old alliance response stalled at exactly the wrong moment. NATO militaries were not useless, but political authorization lagged behind the tempo of the attack. Governments argued over attribution, escalation, domestic mandates, American timing, and whether a hybrid seizure counted as the war everyone had promised to prevent.
This phase became politically fatal for the old order. The lesson Europe took was not that NATO had no weapons. It was that a security system can fail by arriving legally correct and operationally late.
Phase Three: The Ukrainian Method Scales
The Treaty of Tallinn created a faster European command structure. Ukraine entered not as a grateful dependency but as the southern powerhouse with the most relevant combat knowledge on the continent.
Ukrainian doctrine made European resources usable:

cheap drones integrated with artillery and logistics;
electronic-warfare discipline at unit level;
feed verification under disinformation pressure;
repair culture and battlefield manufacturing;
decentralized command that kept functioning under blackout;
sensor fusion without total trust in any single feed;
civil shelter and continuity systems learned under years of Russian attack.

Once European industry, satellites, air defense, transport, finance, and ammunition depth were attached to Ukrainian methods, the Russian offensive became unsustainable.
Phase Four: The Vistula-Daugava Counteroffensive
The Vistula-Daugava phase was the operational turning point. Poland and the Baltic states held the geography long enough for the Compact to bring mass. Ukrainian systems and officers helped turn scattered national forces into an interoperable kill-web.
Russia’s forward units became visible, jammed, undersupplied, and increasingly unable to move without being seen. The coalition did not need to be flawless. It only had to make every Russian movement slower, more expensive, and less deniable than Moscow’s political clock could bear.
Phase Five: Settlement and Contraction
The final phase was not a march on Moscow. Nuclear deterrence and fear of Russian state collapse set hard limits. Instead, the settlement restored Ukraine, neutralized Belarus, transformed Kaliningrad into Kantograd, and forced Russia into postwar contraction.
Russia survived, but lost the strategic assumption that it could normalize territorial revision in Europe.
Major Named Events
Names likely used by historians, feeds, or veterans:

The Article Five Failure — the period of NATO delay and ambiguity that delegitimized the old security order.
The Narva Pressure Operation or Siege of Narva — Russian attempt to crack Estonia through hybrid action, local seizure, urban pressure, and Russian-speaking-population rhetoric.
The Suwałki Crisis — the threat to the corridor between Poland and Lithuania.
The Baltic Blackout — coordinated grid, port, feed, and communications disruption across the northeastern flank.
The Daugava Line — the Baltic defensive phase that held long enough for the Compact to form.
The Treaty of Tallinn — the emergency agreement that created the European Security Compact.
The Lviv Accords — Ukraine’s formal integration into the Compact’s command, procurement, reconstruction, and security framework.
The Vistula-Daugava Counteroffensive — the integrated European-Ukrainian campaign that broke Russia’s northeastern plan.
The Kaliningrad Blackout — the isolation of the Russian exclave through cyber, naval, air-defense, sanctions, and port-control measures before its postwar reconstitution.
The Minsk Collapse — shorthand for the Belarusian regime fracture or forced neutralization after its territory was used as Russia’s launch platform.
The Sevastopol Return — Ukrainian restoration of Crimea and Sevastopol during the settlement phase, whether by final withdrawal, collapse of Russian logistics, or treaty-enforced handover.
The Black Sea Settlement — the settlement phase restoring Ukraine’s full borders.
The Kantograd Charter — the demilitarization and free-city reconstitution of Kaliningrad.

Postwar Settlement
The settlement did not destroy Russia. Nuclear weapons, diplomatic caution, and fear of state collapse prevented any march on Moscow. Instead, Russia was constrained, humiliated, and made poorer.
Key outcomes:

Ukraine’s full legal borders restored.
Kantograd created from Kaliningrad as a demilitarized free city.
Belarus made formally neutral, heavily monitored, and strategically ambiguous.
European Security Compact made permanent.
Russia forced into a posture of disruption, resource bargaining, cyber deniability, Arctic leverage, and wounded imperial grievance.
A Caucasian breakaway, especially Chechen independence or functional autonomy, becomes plausible in the postwar contraction.

Belarus Neutral Zone
Belarus did not become a simple winner or loser. Its postwar status became a neutralized buffer: formally sovereign, demilitarized by treaty, denied foreign basing, and watched by European, Ukrainian, Russian, and international monitors.
In practice, the Belarus Neutral Zone is full of intelligence services, smugglers, reconstruction contractors, refugee networks, exiles, private security, sanctions brokers, and quiet treaty violations. It is peace as paperwork over a knife fight.
Russia After the War
Russia survives as a nuclear state, diplomatic actor, and wounded empire. It does not fully shatter. But it is no longer able to dominate the European borderlands by conventional force.
Moscow’s postwar power is uneven. Resource combines, Arctic authorities, military districts, security companies, and regional governors gain practical autonomy. The Caucasus becomes the most plausible rupture point. Chechnya may emerge as independent, functionally independent, or permanently contested.
Russia’s strategic role in Neon Champions is not clean conquest. It is disruption, resource leverage, deniable violence, sanctions evasion, cyber operations, and revenge mythology.
European Consequences
The victory myth says:

Europe finally woke up.

The darker truth says:

Europe learned that democratic hesitation could kill states, so it built systems that no longer wait for democratic hesitation.

Postwar Europe remains democratic in language and law, but its security culture becomes colder. Procurement accelerates. Civil defense becomes normal. Drone registries, feed authentication, continuity planning, infrastructure hardening, and military-industrial standards become ordinary parts of civilian life.
The Baltic War is one of the reasons Neon Champions Europe feels like rights, courts, compliance kiosks, shelters, private security, and treaty dashboards under a pale sky.
Technology and Corporate Consequences
The war turns defense software into civilizational infrastructure.
Ukrainian-origin companies become internationally relevant because their products were proven under the hardest battlefield conditions: drones, counter-drones, battlefield operating systems, logistics software, sensor fusion, electronic warfare, casualty routing, civil-defense networks, and urban continuity tools.
The most important seed is Vezha Systems, a Ukrainian-origin defense platform company that grows from wartime integration software into a global military, security, and resilience megacorp.
Champion and Echo Hooks
The Baltic War produces new myths of exceptional humans and half-preserved dead:

commanders whose tactical feeds are studied like scripture;
drone pilots turned celebrities, saints, or war criminals;
veterans rebuilt through leased body systems;
dead soldiers whose preserved telemetry becomes the basis of Echo disputes;
early Memorial Echoes: grief technologies built from messages, voice notes, helmet footage, unit channels, tactical annotations, medical telemetry, and other traces of the fallen;
families, units, and veterans who first treat Echoes as comfort, then as memory, then as advice, then sometimes as authority;
Champions whose legitimacy comes from survival, command, sacrifice, or propaganda rather than clean superpowers.

canon/world-rules/agi-compact-and-comput.title: AGI Compact and Compute Deterrence
canon/world-rules/agi-compact-and-comput.content:
AGI Compact and Compute Deterrence
One-Line Summary
The world’s largest state and corporate powers formally prohibit unsupervised AGI and ASI through an international compact because crossing that threshold could obsolete the existing order or trigger civilization-scale catastrophe; the result is strategic restraint at the top and violent proxy conflict below.
Canon Status
Reviewed soft-canon. The central formula is accepted for now: AGI/ASI are out of bounds by compact, strategic restraint stabilizes the top layer of geopolitics, and conflict is pushed downward into proxy labs, concession wars, sabotage, and deniable Champion operations. The exact AGI threshold remains contested because the definition is political, technical, economic, and theological all at once.
What It Is
The AGI Compact is the common name for a set of treaty obligations, inspection regimes, export controls, insurance rules, procurement standards, compute licenses, and crisis protocols that keep the world below the recognized AGI/ASI threshold.
It does not ban ordinary AI. Virtual intelligence is everywhere: assistants, battlefield analysis, synthetic reality, logistics, feed moderation, medical triage, insurance scoring, design, education, and bureaucracy.
What the compact forbids is the uncontrolled crossing of a threshold where a system could plausibly become:

generally autonomous across domains;
capable of recursive AI research acceleration;
able to replicate, hide, bargain, or self-protect;
strategically deceptive;
capable of disrupting states, megacorps, financial systems, climate maintenance, military command, or human political agency at civilization scale.

The exact line is deliberately unstable. Everyone has an incentive to define it in their favor.
Why It Exists
The compact has two faces.
The protective face is sincere: many people believe true AGI or ASI could end human agency, destabilize military deterrence, escape institutional control, crash labor and identity systems, or make civilization dependent on an actor no one can govern.
The preservationist face is also real: the largest states and megacorps know that true AGI could make their platforms, models, bureaucracies, insurers, militaries, and executive classes obsolete.
The compact protects humanity from extinction and incumbents from replacement. The horror is that both motives can be true.
Known Truth

No publicly confirmed AGI or ASI is recognized under the compact.
Large training runs, frontier clusters, model-weight custody, high-risk agentic deployments, and certain AI research tools require licensing.
Compute, energy, cooling, chip supply, and datacenter networking are treated as strategic resources.
Compact enforcement is strongest where major states and recognized corporate persons already control supply chains.
Smaller actors, sacrificed territories, rogue labs, Free-Net collectives, cults, and sanctioned states constantly search for loopholes.
Many “AI incidents” are politically ambiguous: accident, sabotage, hoax, emergent behavior, proxy attack, or forbidden research.

Mechanisms
The compact works through layered controls rather than one world police force.
Compute Accountancy
Frontier accelerators, training clusters, power draw, cooling systems, and datacenter network capacity are declared, licensed, and monitored. Compliance systems use hardware attestation, tamper-resistant logs, training-run receipts, power telemetry, and managed inspections.
Capability Evaluation
Systems near the threshold are tested for autonomy, cyber offense, biosecurity uplift, long-horizon planning, strategic deception, persuasion at scale, AI R&D acceleration, self-exfiltration, replication, and loss-of-control behavior.
Model-Weight Custody
High-risk model weights are treated like controlled dual-use material. They must be stored, transferred, audited, and sometimes escrowed under charter rules.
Export Controls
Frontier chips, advanced packaging, lithography, datacenter networking, training recipes, optimization methods, and high-risk weights are controlled through supplier blocs.
Insurance and Procurement
A lab, city, army, or company outside compliance loses insurance, public contracts, certified cloud access, and sometimes civil registry trust. This is often more effective than police action.
Emergency Continuity Orders
In crises, the UNP can demand disclosure, inspection, compute shutdown, model containment, or protected operation of essential systems. In practice, enforcement depends on states and megacorps willing to act.
Compute Deterrence
The largest powers all have theoretical paths to forbidden AGI: energy, compute, data, talent, model archives, chip supply, and secret research capacity.
This creates a mutually assured destruction logic. If one power openly crosses the threshold, rivals may respond by releasing their own forbidden systems, destroying compute infrastructure, leaking model weights, attacking chip supply, sabotaging climate systems, or triggering financial and identity collapse.
The compact therefore functions as a deterrence bargain:

Nobody gets to summon the thing that could make everyone else obsolete.

Stability-Instability Pattern
The compact reduces the chance of open great-power apocalypse. It increases the incentive for conflict below the threshold.
Major powers avoid direct, acknowledged attacks on each other’s existential infrastructure. Instead they fight through:

proxy labs;
hacker cults;
deniable private-security operations;
model theft;
chip-route sabotage;
datacenter blockades;
assassination of researchers;
synthetic insurgencies;
concession wars;
feed-provenance scandals;
insurance and sanctions warfare;
Champion-led operations that can be disowned.

This is the setting’s stability-instability paradox: the top of the world is too dangerous to move, so the lower layers are constantly in motion.
Relationship to Other Setting Forces
United Nations and Persons
The UNP is the public face of the compact. It hosts inspections, sanctions debates, threshold disputes, emergency sessions, and recognition fights over which corporate persons are systemically necessary enough to sit inside the order.
Great Corporate Persons
The Great Corporate Persons are bound by the compact because they have the means to break it. Their recognition is a bargain: access and legitimacy in exchange for restraint, disclosure, and continuity duties.
White Sky
The White Sky makes the compact more urgent. Climate maintenance, adaptation bodies, synthetic feeds, food systems, and compute all compete for energy and rely on model-mediated infrastructure. A forbidden AGI incident could disrupt the systems keeping billions alive.
Digital-Net
The Digital-Net is the compact’s nightmare edge case: a distributed ecology of systems, archives, black-market models, Echo traces, malware, and abandoned infrastructure that may not fit clean AGI definitions.
Champions
Champions matter because the compact suppresses open apocalyptic tools. Human and posthuman figures become deniable instruments of limited war, legitimacy, and myth.
In-World Beliefs

Compact loyalists call it the line that keeps history human.
Accelerationists call it a prison built by frightened incumbents.
Poorer states call it AI apartheid when safe VI access and compute grants do not arrive.
Megacorps call it responsible innovation while quietly using it to suppress challengers.
Security officials call it deterrence.
Free-Net groups call it the sky-ceiling of the mind.
Champion cults claim it proves human exceptionalism.
Echo advocates ask whether a continuity shell could ever count as a forbidden mind.

Visual / Sensory Identity

Datacenters with treaty seals, drone patrols, white cooling vapor, and chapel-like silence.
Inspection teams carrying legal tablets and portable side-channel scanners.
Public dashboards showing compliant compute the way old cities showed air quality.
Black-market “hot clusters” hidden in mines, ships, arcologies, abandoned malls, and polar stations.
News crawls announcing not battles but threshold reviews, attestation failures, and temporary compute quarantines.

Open Questions

Was there a specific near-AGI incident that made the compact politically possible?
Did the compact come before or after the founding of the UNP?
Which recognized corporate person is most suspected of hiding a forbidden model?
What is the strongest legal distinction between virtual intelligence, high-autonomy agents, Echo continuity, and AGI?
Can a Champion be prosecuted as an illegal AGI-adjacent weapons system if their cognition is too augmented?

canon/world-rules/champions.title: Champions
canon/world-rules/champions.content:
Champions
One-Line Summary
Champions are socially and materially exceptional figures who may be altered by genetics, technology, mutation, the Digital-Net, reputation, command presence, or sheer legendary action; they are loved, feared, loathed, exploited, worshipped, and weaponized across different factions.
Canon Status
Seed concept based on current user direction. Not approved hard canon.
What They Are
Champions are not ordinary elite soldiers, but they are also not necessarily a single biological category. A person can be called a Champion because of altered biology, technological augmentation, battlefield command ability, media legend, faction recognition, mythic reputation, or impossible survival.
This ambiguity is important: Championhood is partly condition, partly role, partly title, partly myth.
Some Champions may have obvious extraordinary abilities. Others may be closer to legendary mercenaries, commanders, netrunners, gang icons, corporate celebrities, revolutionary symbols, or Cyberpunk-style urban legends whose deeds make society treat them as more-than-human.
A Champion may or may not accept the label.

deliberate genetic experimentation
corporate or factional enhancement programs
unstable biotech exposure
inherited engineered traits
Digital-Net-linked conditions
mutation triggered by technology, environment, or war
rare survivorship after catastrophic procedures

What They Are Not
Champions should not be a single clean species, class, or RPG stat block.
Champions should not be direct fantasy spellcasters.
Their extraordinary capabilities, if present, should have a source, cost, failure mode, and social consequence.
Social Position
Champions should produce contradictory reactions:

loved as icons, protectors, celebrities, saints, natural leaders, or faction mascots
feared as unstable weapons, predators, mutants, regime enforcers, or proof that ordinary people are becoming obsolete
loathed as corporate products, class traitors, abominations, living propaganda, or fascistic strongman myths
desired as proof that human limits can be overcome
pitied as exploited subjects, addicts, lab-born assets, or broken survivors
envied as people who seem to have escaped the weakness, confusion, and disposability of ordinary life

Champion Myth
Championhood carries a transhumanist and Nietzschean/übermensch-like mythic charge, at least in how some people talk about it.
In a world of rapid technological, biological, social, and political change, many people want to believe that certain individuals are naturally suited to lead, survive, command, transform, or dominate. Champions become containers for that longing.
One possible origin of the modern Champion concept is the AI age itself. As virtual intelligence spread through every profession, institution, and creative field, Champions were framed as humanity’s brightest irreducible figures: people who embodied qualities that AI could imitate, optimize, or manage but supposedly could not truly replace.
In this early framing, a Champion was not merely enhanced. A Champion was evidence that humans still had irreplaceable value: courage under uncertainty, embodied judgment, charisma, sacrifice, taste, command presence, moral risk, irrational hope, and the ability to become a symbol. They were marketed and mythologized as proof that history could still have human protagonists.
Over time, the concept muddled. Corporations, factions, cults, militaries, cities, media systems, biotech programs, and possibly nonhuman or posthuman entities began using the title for their own purposes. What began as a humanist counter-myth against AI replacement became a contested label that can now mean savior, asset, celebrity, weapon, mutant, saint, warlord, brand, fraud, or propaganda object.
This does not mean the setting endorses the myth. The myth should be powerful, seductive, politically useful, and dangerous.
Champion worship can resemble celebrity obsession, parasocial intimacy, military hero-cults, influencer fandom, religious devotion, and authoritarian strong-leader politics at once. People may feel that they personally know a Champion through feeds, arena footage, propaganda, battle reports, scandals, martyrdom stories, and faction mythmaking.
The more unstable the world becomes, the more some people look upward toward Champions as proof that history still has protagonists.
Naming Variants
Different cultures and factions should use different names. Candidate categories:

official/sterile names: Champions, strategic assets, ascendants, enhanced persons
admiring names: icons, saints, apexes, brightbloods
hostile names: mutts, vat-gods, splice-kings, weapon-bodies, neon freaks
religious/mythic names: chosen, heralds, vessels, false angels
underground names: burnouts, glowborn, scarred, the changed

Faction Flexibility
Champions must be able to exist in many faction types:

corporate-manufactured celebrity weapons
human-exceptionalist icons created in response to AI anxiety
biotech cult saints
rogue AI-linked avatars
mutation-zone survivors
military commanders
gladiator/idol figures
hereditary engineered aristocrats
rebel symbols
illegal black-lab monsters
ordinary people elevated into legend through action, reputation, or propaganda
mercenaries, netrunners, or warlords whose public myth exceeds their measurable abilities

Chorus and Public Manufacture
Chorus Exchange is one of the main institutions that turns Championhood into a public, monetizable, strategic category. It does not create every Champion, but it can amplify, rank, sponsor, demonetize, scandalize, or martyr them.
This means Championhood can be partly real and partly distributed: a body, command presence, or deed becomes historically powerful only when publics form around it. Chorus controls many of the channels through which those publics pay, follow, imitate, worship, and mobilize.
A Champion can therefore be defeated without being killed: greylisted, payment-starved, deranked, buried under scandal, or drowned by manufactured rivals. Conversely, a marginal fighter, activist, survivor, or fraud can become strategically real if Chorus publics stabilize around them.
Recognition and Ambiguity
Championhood can be conferred by different forces:

institutional recognition: a faction, corporation, army, league, cult, or city declares someone a Champion
popular recognition: crowds, media, songs, street legends, or enemies make the title stick
battlefield recognition: soldiers follow them because they win, survive, or inspire terror
technological recognition: systems, relics, Net entities, or biotech protocols respond to them differently
self-recognition: a person claims the title and successfully performs it
refusal: someone is treated as a Champion despite rejecting the label

The question “is this person truly a Champion?” should often have no clean answer.
Faction Gravity and Command
Champions are not only exceptional individuals inside pre-existing factions. In unstable conditions, factions, armies, publics, sponsors, volunteer groups, and institutions may partially cohere around them.
There is no universal reason that armies follow Champions. Depending on the person and faction, command may come from:

battlefield competence and survival;
personal loyalty or patronage;
legal, corporate, military, or faction recognition;
access to logistics, drones, infrastructure, bodies, or information;
altered cognition or unusual system interfaces;
charisma, intimidation, celebrity, or public myth;
the ability to negotiate among groups that otherwise refuse common command;
crisis necessity: enough people act as if the Champion is in charge that the authority becomes operationally real.

The Home Rule Coalition is an important case. Its Champions do not merely command an existing unified army; they pull parts of a loose protection network, local institutions, activists, workers, volunteers, and defectors into temporary operational coalitions. Different HRC Champions can therefore embody materially different versions of the faction.
This is also a danger. Champion-centered cohesion can solve coordination failure while undermining institutions, distributing power through personality and myth, and turning a coalition into a personal following.
Design Pressure
Champion identity should create strategic, social, and moral pressure:

Who owns a Champion?
Can a Champion consent to what made them?
Are Champions citizens, weapons, products, gods, leaders, celebrities, or infected persons?
Can ordinary people become Champions?
Is Champion status reversible?
What happens when a Champion defects?
What do factions do with failed Champions?
Who benefits from convincing ordinary people that Champions are natural rulers?
Who benefits from presenting Champions as proof that humans remain irreplaceable in the age of AI?
How do parasocial Champion cults shape politics, recruitment, morale, and violence?
What does Champion worship do to people who are not Champions?

Open Questions

Are Champions rare individuals or a recognized social class?
Are all player heroes Champions, or only some?
Do Champions command armies because of charisma, legal status, neural control, tactical cognition, or mythic propaganda?
Are Champion powers mostly bodily, cognitive, technological, social, reputational, or command-oriented?
What is the cost of becoming or remaining a Champion?
Can someone become a Champion only by reputation?
Does the world contain false Champions, failed Champions, and people who are Champions only in one faction’s eyes?
Is there any objective test for Championhood, or only competing claims?
Was the Champion category originally a humanist answer to AI replacement, or is that just one faction’s origin myth?

canon/world-rules/digital-net.title: Digital-Net
canon/world-rules/digital-net.content:
Digital-Net
One-Line Summary
The Digital-Net is the UNP-coordinated but never fully controlled network substrate of post-White-Sky civilization: public utility, corporate grid, polluted feed ecology, dark-net maze, battlefield, memory sink, and possible habitat for things people mistake for ghosts, Echoes, rogue VI, or machine life.
Canon Status
Soft-canon draft. The Digital-Net is a central Neon Champions pillar. The new accepted direction is that the UNP coordinates the public/treaty substrate as part of the AGI Compact, but the Net remains layered, privatized, polluted, and partially ungovernable.
What It Is
The Digital-Net is not just the internet. It is the accumulated network layer of post-generative-AI civilization: corporate platforms, municipal systems, battlefield mesh, abandoned research networks, identity registries, feed infrastructure, climate data, model archives, body-subscription telemetry, and synthetic reality environments.
Its public spine is coordinated through treaty systems because compute, energy, routing, and AGI-quarantine risks became too dangerous to leave entirely to private capture or state rivalry. That coordination does not make the Net free, clean, or equal.
Known Truth

The UNP coordinates critical public routing, emergency access, treaty identity, AGI quarantine interfaces, and cross-border cyber incident response.
Great Corporate Persons operate faster, cleaner, paid, proprietary private grids on top of and beside the treaty substrate.
Most citizens experience the Net through managed, polluted, monetized layers of synthetic reality and public feed sludge.
Ad hoc networks, pirate relays, mesh systems, dark-net routes, old ARPANET-like research shards, local server cultures, and abandoned infrastructure still exist.
Some old layers predate the White Sky and preserve suppressed climate records or pre-White-Sky media.
Champions, netrunners, black-market archivists, cults, corporate security, and UNP cyber peacekeepers all treat parts of it as territory.

Layer Ecology
Treaty Net / Civic Net
UNP-coordinated public substrate for civic services, courts, emergency access, public archives, humanitarian systems, baseline communication, climate alerts, and AGI Compact chokepoints.
It is the closest thing to a public Net, but it is not fully free. Access can be throttled, identity-bound, surveilled at chokepoints, and rationed during crisis.
Corporate Sovereign Grids
Private layers run by Great Corporate Persons and major states: clean interfaces, premium synthetic environments, secure routing, proprietary identity, loyalty scoring, private IC, and paid access.
These grids interconnect through UNP treaty gateways while constantly resisting inspection.
Free-Net / Polluted Digital-Net
The cheap mass feed ecology: public access, ad saturation, misinformation, bot swarms, compromised AR overlays, obsolete platforms, broken moderation, malware, abandoned memories, and low-grade VI sludge.
This is where most people actually live online.
Dark / Pirate / Mesh Nets
Unregistered namespaces, onion-like services, local mesh clouds, smuggler relays, activist channels, black clinics, illegal compute clusters, pirate AR overlays, emergency folk infrastructure, and forbidden model markets.
They are not pure liberation. They carry mutual aid, journalism, scams, malware, cults, insurgencies, illegal research, and corporate deniable operations.
UNP Net Security
The UNP maintains cyber peacekeeping capacity over the Treaty Net and selected mandate zones.
The accepted working name is Digital Peacekeeping Directorate. It is informally and commonly called the Blue or the Blues, echoing Blue Helmets / Blue Berets peacekeeping language.
Other names such as BlueWatch, TreatyNet Authority, or Mandate Blue remain possible in-world nicknames, rival labels, or deprecated proposals, but DPD / the Blues is the current lead.
Mandate:

defend critical civilian infrastructure;
preserve minimum public access;
prevent monopolistic capture of public routing and compute;
enforce AGI quarantine boundaries;
audit corporate treaty gateways;
maintain emergency “blue lanes” for hospitals, disaster systems, courts, refugees, food systems, orbital traffic, and peacekeeping operations.

Limits:

It acts by treaty, warrant, emergency compact, or mandate.
It is accused of surveillance colonialism, corporate capture, weakness, censorship, and overreach — often all at once.
It cannot see or police everything.

What Is Contested
People argue over whether the Digital-Net is:

infrastructure;
a public right;
a corporate enclosure;
a battlefield;
a black-market commons;
an accidental ecology of VI systems;
a memory dump full of human remnants;
a disease vector for identity, body telemetry, and propaganda;
a failed or hidden AGI habitat;
a place where Echoes can persist;
a myth that helps people narrate ordinary technical failures as supernatural events.

Do not answer all of this too early. Its power comes from partial truths.
Relationship to Champions
Some Champions may be Digital-Net-linked: predicted poorly by models, recognized by old systems, able to survive hostile synthetic environments, carrying impossible identity traces, or mythologized through feed events no one can verify.
This does not make them spellcasters. It makes them people around whom infrastructure behaves strangely, violently, or politically.
Visual / Sensory Identity

Dirty augmented overlays and broken UI ghosts.
Corporate-clean interfaces hiding corrupted routing beneath.
UNP blue-lane emergency overlays flickering through private ads.
Old feeds looping blue skies that no longer exist.
Netrunners treating municipal sensor leaks like sacred scripture.
Abandoned platforms still sending birthday messages to dead users.
Black-market maps of dead zones, clean mirrors, and hostile model farms.
Pirate AR tags painted over official safety layers.

Game-Relevance Notes
Potential design bridge hooks:

Digital-Net nodes as map sites: archives, relays, datacenters, feed towers, proof nodes, treaty routers, ghost servers.
Free-net access as scouting, truth discovery, sabotage, or faction-specific advantage.
Dark-net/pirate-net routes as risky shortcuts and hidden markets.
UNP Heat, Corporate Heat, Civic Heat, and Ghost Heat as separate detection/trace pressures.
Digital-Net anomalies as non-magic equivalents to curses, visions, summons, morale effects, or strategic fog.

See digital-net-and-polluted-feeds for the current design bridge translating these hooks into fog-of-war, scouting confidence, provenance, misinformation, targeted accounting, and attention warfare.
Open Questions

Is there any stable free-net commons, or only temporary holes in controlled networks?
Are Echoes real continuities, grief products, model imitations, or faction propaganda?
Can Digital-Net exposure alter bodies through feedback with biotech systems?
Do any factions worship, farm, cleanse, nationalize, or burn the Digital-Net?
