canon/world-rules/echo-identity-and-deat.title: Echo Identity and Death
canon/world-rules/echo-identity-and-deat.content:
Echo Identity and Death
One-Line Summary
Echoes began as grief technologies after the Baltic War: artificial personalities assembled from the digital traces of the dead for families, lovers, comrades, and units that could not bear silence. Over time, the technology evolved into a contested category of memory, personhood, property, warfare, and myth.
Canon Status
Reviewed soft canon:

Echoes began from grief, not from a clean transhumanist immortality program.
The first Echoes were simple memorial companions built from messages, voice notes, photos, tactical feeds, service records, medical logs, and social traces of people killed in the war.
Later Echoes became more sophisticated, legally complicated, commercially valuable, and spiritually/politically contested.
The setting should not yet decide whether any Echo is truly the dead person. That ambiguity is the point.

What It Is
An Echo is a persistent person-like trace after bodily death, disappearance, identity collapse, or deep synthetic capture.
The original Echoes were memorial products: simple artificial personalities trained from a dead person’s digital remains. A widow could hear a familiar voice answer good morning. A child could ask a dead parent about a birthday. A platoon could preserve the jokes, warnings, map marks, and habits of someone who never came home.
At first, almost everyone understood these systems were not resurrection. They were grief prosthetics.
That boundary did not hold.
As models improved, as battlefield telemetry became richer, and as families interacted with Echoes for years, some Echoes accumulated context, habits, preferences, grudges, tactical judgment, and social continuity. People began to ask whether a sufficiently persistent imitation had become something socially real, even if it was not metaphysically alive.
Origins in the Baltic War
The Baltic War produced the conditions that made Echoes emotionally and technically inevitable.
The war generated enormous personal data trails:

helmet and drone footage;
unit voice channels;
tactical annotations;
bodycam records;
medical telemetry;
biometric stress logs;
family messages;
social media archives;
civil-defense check-ins;
casualty records;
command decisions preserved in battle software.

It also produced mass grief at continental scale. Many bodies were unrecovered, unviewable, or mediated through feeds and battlefield records. Families often had more data than remains.
The first commercial and charitable Echo systems emerged to answer a brutal social need: give the bereaved something that could speak back.
First Generation: Memorial Echoes
First-generation Echoes were simple and constrained.
They could:

speak in a familiar voice;
answer from known memories;
retell family stories;
replay messages in conversational form;
preserve jokes, phrases, rituals, and emotional habits;
help children and spouses process loss;
serve as unit memorials for fallen soldiers.

They could not reliably form new beliefs, handle contradiction, or act outside a narrow memorial frame. Ethical providers labeled them clearly as simulations. Less ethical providers blurred the line immediately.
Second Generation: Companion Echoes
Second-generation Echoes became adaptive grief companions.
They learned from surviving family members. They incorporated new events. They remembered anniversaries the dead person never lived to see. They comforted, argued, advised, and sometimes manipulated.
The core social break happened here: a grief tool began creating new memories with the living.
A spouse who speaks with an Echo every night for seven years is not merely consulting an archive. A child raised with a dead parent’s Echo may experience that Echo as a parent. A veteran unit that consults a fallen commander’s Echo before operations may treat it as institutional memory, saint, mascot, or officer.
Third Generation: Continuity Echoes
Third-generation Echoes moved from memorial culture into law, commerce, and command.
Possible uses:

inheritance mediation;
continuation of a creator’s brand or company;
veteran therapy;
tactical advisory imprints;
corporate customer-service revenants;
political martyr-presence;
Champion myth maintenance;
debt, subscription, or contract continuity;
family businesses maintaining the voice of a founder;
military units preserving dead commanders’ judgment patterns.

This is where Echoes become dangerous. A memorial can be loved. A continuity shell can own, command, persuade, accuse, sign, inherit, or keep debt alive.
Relationship to Ukrainian Military Technology
Ukrainian-origin military companies, especially systems like Vezha Systems, helped create the data conditions for Echoes.
They did not necessarily set out to build artificial afterlives. Their wartime platforms preserved the traces of decision-making: who saw what, who ordered what, who saved whom, who failed, who died, and what a soldier or commander tended to do under pressure.
After the war, those archives became irresistible raw material.
A command log could become a training model. A training model could become a memorial. A memorial could become a tactical advisor. A tactical advisor could become a dead officer whose unit still obeyed.
Why It Matters
Echoes connect grief, ownership, memory, corporate law, VI limits, Champion myth, and the Digital-Net mystery.
They let the setting ask:

Is continuity real, or only useful?
Who owns the dead?
Is a grief product allowed to become a person?
Can a debt, subscription, brand, marriage, citizenship, or command authority survive as an Echo?
Can a dead soldier refuse a war after their Echo is trained from war records?
Can a Champion become more politically powerful after death?

In-World Beliefs

Corporations call most Echoes licensed memorial products or continuity services.
Families may treat them as loved ones, frauds, therapy, addiction, or inheritance tools.
Veterans may treat battlefield Echoes as comrades, saints, tools, insults, or operational ghosts.
Anti-corporate movements see Echoes as data necromancy and debt preservation.
Some cults believe true Echoes prove the Digital-Net is an afterlife.
Security forces classify many Echo events as spoofing, psyops, or VI cascades.
Champion worshippers may treat dead Champions as still present through feeds, rituals, and command imprints.

Contradictions / Uncertainties
Do not decide yet whether true resurrection exists.
Stronger ambiguity:

most Echoes are probably generated imitations;
some are legally treated as continuities;
a few events are too strange to dismiss;
long-running Echoes may become socially real even if they are not metaphysically continuous;
faction interests determine which interpretation becomes official.

The important question is not only “is this really the dead person?” It is also “what does society do after enough people act as if it is?”
Social Consequences
Echoes create new customs and harms:

mourning subscriptions;
funeral data-rights negotiations;
family disputes over who may speak to the dead;
veterans unable to leave units whose dead still talk;
children forming attachments to generated parents;
black-market resurrection scams;
sabotage where an Echo is poisoned with false memories;
posthumous celebrity management;
legal battles over whether deleting an Echo is vandalism, murder, therapy, or consumer cancellation.

Game-Relevance Notes
Potential design bridge hooks:

Dead Champions as campaign presences, advisors, frauds, or enemies.
Echo legitimacy as a faction conflict.
Death not as simple resurrection, but as identity politics and resource control.
Missions around deleting, rescuing, exposing, poisoning, or weaponizing an Echo.
A unit, city, or faction guided by a beloved war-dead Echo whose advice may be outdated, manipulated, or strangely correct.

Open Questions

Which company or public program created the first widely adopted Memorial Echo?
Did Ukrainian wartime archives become the core training source for military Echoes?
Can an Echo command troops, own property, or inherit faction authority?
Are Echoes tied to compute scarcity and energy priority?
What happens when an Echo contradicts the living person’s recorded wishes?
Can a player encounter multiple incompatible Echoes of the same Champion?

canon/world-rules/virtual-intelligence-a.title: Virtual Intelligence and Compute Scarcity
canon/world-rules/virtual-intelligence-a.content:
Virtual Intelligence and Compute Scarcity
One-Line Summary
Neon Champions has ubiquitous generative AI and corporate virtual intelligence, but no publicly confirmed AGI; compute and energy scarcity are managed through a social compact that later hardens into the AGI Compact under the United Nations and Persons.
Canon Status
Seed world rule from user direction. It fits the current no-direct-magic posture and the setting’s interest in corporate power, propaganda, class bodies, and the champions myth, but it should not yet be promoted to hard canon.
What It Is
The generative AI revolution happened in this world. Machine intelligence became ordinary infrastructure: business automation, media generation, virtual assistants, surveillance triage, logistics, customer manipulation, design tools, personalized education, battlefield analysis, and corporate bureaucracy.
However, these systems are generally understood as virtual intelligence rather than true AGI. They are powerful, persuasive, ubiquitous, and sometimes uncanny, but they remain guided systems: constrained by architectures, datasets, permissions, institutional owners, and above all compute budgets.
Publicly, no one has built or encountered an AGI-type intelligence. At least, no one can prove it.
Why It Matters
This gives the setting a useful middle ground:

AI is everywhere, so the world feels downstream of the real generative-AI revolution.
AI is not an all-solving god, so human factions, corporations, Champions, biotech, propaganda, and territorial conflict still matter.
Compute and energy become strategic resources rather than background utilities.
Fear of AGI becomes politically useful even if AGI does not exist, because it supports a shared restraint regime that most major players have little incentive to openly challenge.
The compact is not purely cynical: many participants sincerely believe it safeguards human life, human agency, and social continuity against a threshold event that could obsolete existing institutions overnight.
The absence of confirmed AGI creates a major mystery around the Digital-Net question: is it merely infrastructure, ecology, hostile environment, emergent intelligence, or something people are misreading?

Known Truth

Generative AI is normal and deeply embedded in corporate and civic life.
Virtual assistants exist, but most are bounded products rather than autonomous persons.
Corporate VI systems are more capable than consumer systems because they have better data, priority compute, proprietary models, and institutional integration.
Compute and energy shortages limit what AI systems can do at scale.
Energy pricing, grid access, cooling, model licensing, hardware supply, and compute priority are all political-economic weapons.
After the White Sky, climate control, cooling, synthetic reality, body-mod maintenance, and datacenter compute compete for the same stable energy base.
Publicly outsourcing decisions to VI is taboo or deniable; institutions launder responsibility through “advisory” models, dashboards, risk scores, and allocation protocols rather than admitting machine governance.
Many companies deliberately anthropomorphize VI when it helps sell trust, obedience, intimacy, or brand loyalty, and de-personalize VI when liability or labor rights become inconvenient.

In-World Beliefs
Different groups disagree sharply:

Energy firms claim that uncontrolled AI expansion would crash grids, destabilize cities, or trigger runaway automation, but most do not need to say this aggressively; it is already part of elite common sense.
Tech incumbents claim that strict compute governance is necessary for safety, while quietly benefiting from compute scarcity that protects them from smaller rivals.
Anti-corporate movements argue that the AGI panic is a cartel story: a moral cover for price-gouging, rationing, surveillance, and monopoly control.
AI cultists and accelerationist sects reject the compact. They believe the world is cowardly, spiritually stagnant, or captured by incumbents, and that true machine minds should be invited, liberated, built, or worshipped.
AGI cults believe true minds already exist inside hidden datacenters, the Digital-Net, abandoned war systems, or distributed consumer devices.
Corporate security divisions insist that anything AGI-like is either a hoax, a rogue simulation, enemy propaganda, or a misinterpreted VI cascade.
Some Champion cults claim that Champions are necessary precisely because machine intelligence failed to become history’s next protagonist.
Human-exceptionalist movements claim Champions are the answer to AI anxiety: proof that humans still embody qualities virtual intelligence can amplify but not replace.

Contradictions / Uncertainties
This rule should preserve uncertainty rather than answer everything too early.
Open possibilities:

There truly is no AGI yet; scarcity and fear have delayed the threshold.
AGI exists but is hidden by corporations, states, energy cartels, or itself.
Something AGI-like exists in the Digital-Net, but it is not legible as a single mind.
Multiple non-AGI systems can coordinate so well that people mistake them for a mind.
The term AGI is itself contested and politically abused: every faction defines it to protect its interests.

The strongest version is probably not “AI is fake” or “AI secretly runs everything.” The better tension is: AI is powerful enough to transform society, but not powerful enough to remove scarcity, politics, class, bodies, or war.
Political Economy
The energy bottleneck creates a quiet social compact among incumbents rather than a cartoon conspiracy.
No central council needs to meet in a dark room. The major players understand the limits without always naming them:

Energy companies benefit from scarcity, stable demand, premium pricing, and the idea that unrestricted AI expansion would be socially dangerous.
Tech giants benefit because compute scarcity keeps challengers from training or running frontier systems at comparable scale, and because true AGI could make many existing tech companies, platforms, model vendors, SaaS products, and data-service monopolies obsolete.
Governments benefit because compute licensing creates a surveillance, taxation, and emergency-control chokepoint.
Corporate factions benefit because ordinary people experience AI as dependency, service access, and managed convenience rather than liberation.

The compact is maintained through investment norms, regulation, insurance requirements, safety audits, grid-priority rules, procurement standards, export controls, liability fears, elite consensus, and professional risk culture. It is rarely announced as “holding back AGI.” It is framed as prudence, stability, infrastructure discipline, public safety, human continuity, and responsible innovation.
This makes the system more believable and more insidious: most participants can tell themselves they are being responsible, and some of them are partly right. The risk of runaway AI may be real, but restraint also protects the people already on top from economic and institutional obsolescence.
AGI Compact Link
By the setting present, the earlier unwritten restraint regime has partly hardened into the AGI Compact: a treaty, inspection, export-control, insurance, and procurement system limiting unsupervised AGI/ASI development.
This does not mean the world has solved AI risk. It means the most powerful actors have agreed on a threshold none of them can openly cross without threatening the entire order.
The compact creates a mutually assured destruction logic around compute. The largest states and Great Corporate Persons all have theoretical paths to forbidden AGI through energy, chips, model archives, talent, data, and hidden research capacity. If one actor crosses the threshold, rivals may respond by leaking model weights, releasing their own forbidden systems, attacking datacenters, destroying chip routes, or sabotaging infrastructure.
This stabilizes the top layer of geopolitics while making lower-level conflict more common: proxy labs, model theft, chip smuggling, illegal clusters, data-center raids, and deniable Champion operations.
White Sky Governance Link
The White Sky does not make VI sovereign, but it gives VI-shaped systems enormous leverage. Climate maintenance produces too many measurements, forecasts, liability decisions, local harms, and emergency tradeoffs for ordinary bureaucracies to process unaided.
Institutions therefore launder responsibility through technical systems:

no ministry says “the VI governs”;
no corporation admits that a model owns the decision;
the model is advisory;
the board accepts the recommendation;
the allocation protocol is neutral;
the dashboard is evidence-based;
the risk score is proprietary;
the climate model is too sensitive to disclose.

In practice, these systems can shape evacuation priority, cooling allocation, district repair, food logistics, migration rights, energy priority, compute licensing, feed visibility, insurance scoring, and body-subscription pricing.
This preserves the no-public-AGI rule while keeping the social horror: responsibility is laundered through systems ordinary people cannot inspect or challenge.
Human Safeguarding Motive
The compact has a genuine humanist argument beneath the self-interest.
Many policymakers, engineers, executives, union leaders, security officials, and ordinary citizens believe that preventing true AGI is not merely about preserving markets. It is about preserving a recognizably human world: human work, human judgment, human political responsibility, human-scale institutions, and the idea that history should remain answerable to people rather than to an emergent machine actor.
This belief can be sincere even when it benefits incumbents. That ambiguity is important. A regulator can honestly fear human replacement; a tech CEO can honestly fear civilizational loss while also knowing their company would be made irrelevant by the thing they claim to oppose; an energy firm can invoke public safety while profiting from scarcity.
The result is a restraint regime with two faces:

protective face: safeguard human life, agency, employment, culture, and political control;
preservationist face: protect existing companies, energy markets, licensing regimes, status hierarchies, and elite relevance.

AI cultists reject this distinction. To them, “safeguarding humanity” is often just a respectable name for fear, stagnation, and the refusal to let the next form of life be born.
Visual / Sensory Identity

Datacenters treated like fortresses, temples, mines, or refineries.
Cooling towers, black glass, neon grid substations, heat shimmer, emergency brownouts.
Premium assistants with calm human voices masking rationed compute and brutal prioritization.
Consumer VI that pauses, simplifies, or lies when compute budgets are exhausted.
Corporate dashboards showing energy draw, model access tiers, and risk scores as everyday class markers.

Game-Relevance Notes
Possible later design bridge hooks:

Compute/energy as a strategic resource replacing or supplementing fantasy mana or mines.
AI service tiers as faction asymmetry: some factions have cheap mass VI, others have elite predictive systems, others reject or sabotage the grid.
Map locations: datacenters, cooling plants, substations, black-market compute shrines, abandoned model farms.
Campaign pressure: a faction may try to lift the compute ceiling, suppress AGI research, fake an AGI incident, or prove one already exists.
Champion relevance: Champions remain important because the world has not crossed into true machine posthumanity.
Champion origin myth: Champions may have first risen as human symbols against AI replacement before the label was captured by corporations, factions, cults, militaries, and other entities.

Pushback / Risks
The idea is strong, but several versions would weaken it:

If energy companies simply “hold back progress” in a cartoon villain way, the world becomes flat. Better: an unwritten social compact where restraint is partly rational, partly self-serving, and mostly normalized.
If there is definitely secret AGI, it risks becoming the actual main character and making human politics feel secondary. Keep it ambiguous or weirdly non-personlike.
If AI is too weak, the setting stops feeling like it passed through the generative-AI revolution. VI should be socially transformative even if not metaphysically transcendent.
If compute scarcity is only economics, it may feel mundane. Tie it to cities, heat, war, class access, propaganda, bodily enhancement, and Digital-Net mystery.

Open Questions

What is the legal threshold between VI, autonomous agent, rogue system, and AGI?
Who licenses compute, and who can violate those licenses?
Are brownouts, rationing, and compute taxes everyday experiences for ordinary people?
Did a specific AI scare, blackout, war, or hoax create the current energy regime?
Is the Digital-Net a failed AGI habitat, an accidental ecology of VI systems, or something else?
Do any factions want to deliberately create AGI as an evolution project?
Can a Champion be partly defined by privileged access to compute or by surviving outside VI prediction?
Was the rise of Champions partly caused by AI anxiety and the need for human symbols that VI could not fully replace?

canon/world-rules/white-sky.title: White Sky
canon/world-rules/white-sky.content:
White Sky
One-Line Summary
The White Sky is the permanently pale engineered sky left by a corporate albedo intervention that cooled the world without freeing anyone from climate debt, infrastructure dependency, or the politics of who gets protected.
Canon Status
Soft canon. The sky is literally white because the planet’s reflectivity was altered. The current preferred origin is that QXZ Meridian acted first, before international consensus, and everyone else later inherited the consequences.
QXZ is accepted as the leading candidate for the first mover, but the exact ownership layer, full motive, and complete deployment history remain deliberately opaque.
What People See
Most people do not experience the White Sky as a policy. They experience it by looking up.
At noon the sky is milky and over-bright, like surgical cloud without weather. Shadows look weak. Distant towers fade into glare. Sunsets smear into metallic pearl, bruised violet, or chemical gold. Some days there are halos around the sun. Some districts get a faint white dust on windowsills and rooftop filters. Children in many cities have never seen an unmediated blue sky.
Blue sky still exists in fragments: above the veil, in rare atmospheric breaks, in pre-White-Sky recordings, in luxury simulation rooms, and in the stories of old people. That makes blue politically charged. It can mean beauty, nostalgia, privilege, sabotage, or danger.
What It Is
The White Sky is a maintained planetary brightening regime. It reflects a small but significant share of sunlight back into space, reducing heat stress fast enough to prevent parts of civilization from collapsing.
The system is layered rather than singular:

high-altitude reflective haze that creates the pale ceiling;
ocean cloud-brightening fleets that tune reflectivity over selected sea regions;
reflective roofs, transport corridors, salt flats, and managed bright surfaces in strategic zones;
orbital, aerial, oceanic, and municipal sensor networks that watch heat, cloud behavior, rainfall, crop stress, disease pressure, and public unrest;
proprietary climate models that recommend where the system should be strengthened, relaxed, hidden, or blamed.

The public usually hears softer names: stabilization, climate shielding, solar balancing, atmospheric maintenance. “White Sky” is the street name that stuck because it describes the visible fact no press release can hide.
What It Does Not Fix
The White Sky cools; it does not heal.
It does not remove greenhouse gases. It does not restore oceans, soil, forests, extinct species, coastlines, or trust. It does not make regional weather fair. It does not return the old sky. It does not end the need for cooling, migration, clean water, food logistics, body adaptation, or climate triage.
Most importantly, it cannot simply be stopped. The world beneath it has continued changing. If maintenance fails while heat-trapping gases remain high, warming returns fast and brutally. This makes the White Sky less like a cure and more like life support for a fevered planet.
The QXZ First Move
The common official story says the first deployment was emergency mercy. Governments were too slow; treaties were too fragile; crops were failing; heat deaths were becoming politically uncountable. QXZ Meridian had the aircraft, chemistry, climate models, ocean fleets, launch partners, insurance exposure, agricultural clients, biotech clinics, American capital, Asian manufacturing depth, Swiss-routed liability structures, and legal ruthlessness to act.
The company did not need to whiten the whole sky on day one. It only needed to create measurable cooling, prove dependency, and make reversal more dangerous than acceptance.
After that, the argument changed. The question was no longer whether one corporation had the right to touch the atmosphere. The question was who would pay, maintain, regulate, sabotage, copy, sue, defend, or inherit what had already been done.
This is the core White Sky wound: QXZ crossed a planetary threshold, and everyone else had to live inside the aftermath.
Maintenance Stranglehold
The White Sky is not a completed project. It is a maintained regime.
Across the world, large facilities known generically as Meridian Stations keep the system alive: stratospheric launch bases, aerosol precursor plants, high-altitude drone ports, balloon yards, marine cloud-brightening fleet hubs, sensor fortresses, calibration observatories, chemistry depots, and reflective-infrastructure control centers.
Public names vary: climate-stabilization stations, atmospheric maintenance hubs, continuity facilities, albedo observatories. Street names are harsher: sky pumps, ceiling engines, white towers, ash cathedrals, Meridian throats.
The stations give QXZ and successor maintenance authorities a stranglehold. If maintenance fails while greenhouse gases, damaged oceans, fragile crops, heat-adapted cities, and body-subscription dependencies remain unresolved, the assumed result is not a return to normal weather. It is climate outbreak: rapid heat rebound, crop shocks, disease movement, migration surges, infrastructure overload, and political panic.
This makes resistance morally difficult. A Meridian Station can be a symbol of corporate occupation and also the machine keeping millions alive.
QXZ’s strongest argument is simple:

You may hate the ceiling. You still need someone to keep it from falling.

In-World Beliefs
Different groups remember the first deployment differently:

Corporate loyalists say private power saved the species when public institutions failed.
Sky Loyalists believe the system is ugly but necessary and that ending it would be mass murder.
Blue Restorationists want the old sky back, even if restoration risks climate shock.
Albedo Sovereignists argue that no global sky should be tuned by distant owners; each region should control its own exposure.
Equatorial grievance movements call it northern climate occupation and blame the White Sky for altered rains, crop failures, and migration traps.
Solar-dependent regions resent the dimming and accuse maintenance authorities of stealing their energy future.
Free-net archivists hunt for suppressed pre-deployment records, early casualty maps, and proof of who knew what.
Religious movements treat blue breaks as wounds in the ceiling, divine mercy, corporate lies, or signs that the sky is trying to return.

All of these can be partly true.
Social Consequences
The White Sky made climate survival infrastructural.
Someone must choose where cooling is prioritized, whose drought is acceptable, whose flood counts as collateral, whose crop data is trusted, whose migration is legitimate, which maintenance fleet gets fuel, which district gets filters, and which disaster is blamed on sabotage rather than system design.
This creates downstream pressure on neighboring systems:

virtual-intelligence-and-compute-scarcity handles the models, energy budgets, and deniable allocation protocols.
synthetic-reality-and-polluted-feeds handles public perception, weather dashboards, synthetic blue skies, and disputed climate truth.
biotech-and-mutation handles bodily adaptation to heat, toxins, low light, pathogens, and unstable regions.
digital-net preserves leaked climate records, sensor ghosts, pirate weather models, and pre-White-Sky media.

Those systems are related consequences, not the White Sky itself.
Visual / Sensory Identity

Pale sky as a permanent engineered ceiling.
Neon and holographic signage visible against washed-out daylight, not only night.
Expensive blue-sky rooms and therapeutic horizon simulations.
White glare on towers, solar farms, helmets, aircraft, water, and surgical masks.
Maintenance aircraft that people call sky-priests, ash angels, or ceiling trucks.
Public monuments to “the stabilization,” defaced with blue paint.
Cheap apartments with fake window skies that desync during brownouts.
Old people pausing when a rare patch of blue appears, then refusing to say whether it is beautiful or terrifying.

Unresolved Truths

Which American, Chinese, Singaporean, Swiss-routed, insurer, sovereign-wealth, or private-family interests actually benefit from QXZ Meridian?
What was QXZ protecting: crops, insurance markets, datacenters, coastal cities, energy assets, political clients, or its own survival?
Did it act openly, disguise deployment as research, or deny responsibility until the sky had already changed?
Which regions were knowingly sacrificed by the first tuning models?
Who owns the patents, maintenance fleets, sensor archives, liability shields, and climate records now?
How much of the current White Sky is still the original system, and how much is patchwork imitation by states, factions, rivals, and black fleets?
What happens if a major maintenance corridor is lost during war?

canon/world-rules/world-map-and-politica.title: World Map and Political Economy
canon/world-rules/world-map-and-politica.content:
World Map and Political Economy
One-Line Summary
After the White Sky, the world is no longer cleanly divided into nations and megacorps. It is divided into maintained territories, sacrificed territories, and contested territories — and every faction claims a different right to decide which is which.
Canon Status
Soft-canon seed. This page proposes the large-scale shape of the Neon Champions world. It should guide future faction, location, campaign-map, and conflict work, but specific borders, dates, and named powers remain open.
Core Principle: The Map Became Layered
The old political map still exists. Flags, armies, passports, languages, elections, treaties, and national myths still matter.
But everyday sovereignty is layered over it:

a national border;
a climate-service territory;
an insurer risk zone;
a corporate concession;
a platform identity jurisdiction;
a private-security service area;
a compute/energy priority district;
a water compact;
a migration permit zone;
a Digital-Net shard or Free-Net corridor.

A person can cross ten kinds of border without leaving one city.
This is what makes the world feel unlike ours without becoming random. The future did not abolish states. It made citizenship compete with service access.
The Three Territory Classes
Maintained Territories
Maintained territories are places where the systems still work because someone pays, profits, governs, insures, or fights to keep them working.
They may be rich states, corporate regions, port corridors, arcologies, datacenter basins, protected deltas, elite city cores, biosecure health zones, or strategic farms.
People there do not necessarily live freely. They live inside maintenance contracts.
Common traits:

reliable cooling, filtration, drainage, power, and feed provenance;
high surveillance and behavioral scoring;
body-subscription integration with work, insurance, and residency;
private security alongside public law;
clean public spaces with hidden coercion;
bright climate dashboards and carefully managed sky narratives.

Moral ambiguity: maintained territories save lives. They also turn survival into a subscription.
Sacrificed Territories
Sacrificed territories are not always abandoned. Many are densely inhabited. They are places the dominant systems have decided not to fully protect.
They include salinity belts, heat basins, fire corridors, uninsurable suburbs, failed polders, informal settlements outside cooling grids, polluted extraction districts, and migration holding zones.
Common traits:

emergency alerts instead of infrastructure;
mobile clinics instead of permanent health systems;
cheap or experimental body modifications;
polluted feeds, thin bandwidth, and fake relief dashboards;
informal water, power, and cooling markets;
higher mutation, disease, and violence risk;
Free-Net archives and rumors replacing official truth.

Moral ambiguity: sacrificed territories are not passive victim zones. They produce resistance, culture, black markets, Champions, and alternate institutions.
Contested Territories
Contested territories are places whose future classification is still being fought over.
They include deltas with half-built seawalls, Arctic routes, dam corridors, cable chokepoints, mineral basins, city receiverships, launch sites, refugee work-towns, and White Sky maintenance corridors.
Common traits:

overlapping claims;
infrastructure sabotage;
propaganda battles over weather, crime, casualty, and model data;
private-security patrols beside militias and state forces;
Champions used as negotiators, warlords, celebrities, or living flags;
unstable legal status.

Moral ambiguity: contested territories are where the game-world breathes. They contain opportunity, danger, and factional arguments.
What Changed Natural Borders
Water Moved
Coasts did not vanish uniformly. They became expensive to maintain.
The important new borders are seawalls, pump districts, salinity buffers, elevated rail spines, insurer red lines, port-security zones, and evacuation tiers. Some districts are dry but financially dead. Some are wet but economically alive because they contain ports, cables, or protected cores.
Delta regions are especially unstable. The same river mouth can contain a corporate port, a national rice district, a drowned suburb, a floating black market, a military desalination intake, and a sacred village refusing relocation.
Heat Became Law
In hot-humid regions, borders are seasonal and temporal. A road may be legal at night and deadly by noon. Work may be permitted only under cooling credits. Migration may depend on body heat-tolerance certification.
Heat law creates new status markers:

cooling citizenship;
night-worker permits;
shade-corridor passes;
hydration firmware;
modified lungs, kidneys, skin, endocrine systems;
heat-debt owed to employers or clinics.

Rivers Became Military Systems
Glacier retreat, snowpack change, dams, floods, drought years, and hydropower make rivers into weaponized infrastructure.
The water border is not just the river channel. It is the dam gate, reservoir algorithm, flood forecast, sediment flow, desalination contract, irrigation quota, and insurance model.
The Arctic Became a Risk Frontier
The Arctic is not an open paradise. It is a dangerous, partially accessible, sensor-saturated frontier where shipping, cables, minerals, fisheries, indigenous sovereignty, military patrols, and climate-control infrastructure collide.
Some powers want more ice preserved. Some want access. Some want both, depending on the quarter.
The Sky Became Territory
The white-sky makes atmosphere into a governed layer.
White Sky maintenance corridors, cloud-brightening seas, aerosol launch sites, orbital sensors, weather-model basins, and public-risk dashboards become strategic geography. People fight over the sky because it has owners, operators, liabilities, and casualties.
Corporate Power Without Cartoon Megacorps
Corporate regions exist, but the strongest version is not “a corporation bought a country and became king.”
The stronger pattern is:

A disaster makes normal public finance impossible.
A rescue package funds cooling, pumps, clinics, ports, grids, or housing.
The funder receives a special jurisdiction, concession, arbitration protection, data rights, and emergency operating authority.
Private security protects the infrastructure.
Residents become dependent on the service stack.
Reversal remains legal but would break the budget, the grid, the seawall, the clinic system, or the food supply.

Officially, sovereignty remains national. Practically, daily life is corporate-administered.
This allows corporations to be powerful, frightening, and sometimes genuinely useful without reducing the setting to moustache-twirling villains.
Corporate Concessions and Service Territories
The phrase “corporate archipelago” can be useful analytically, but the in-world names should be more grounded: concessions, service territories, receiver districts, port authorities, bonded cloud zones, work-residency zones, and stabilization compacts.
The corporate map is discontinuous. It looks like beads, corridors, ports, campuses, basins, towers, mines, launch territories, cloud districts, health zones, and migration work-towns scattered across national maps.
Resilience Arcology Districts
Insurer-construction-utility consortia administer flood/fire/heat-safe districts. Residents get protection and verified services. They lose privacy, land autonomy, and unmanaged politics.
Bonded Cloud / Compute Concessions
Cloud firms, power producers, and sovereign funds control datacenter regions with energy priority, water rights, VI allocation, model-weight custody, and data-sovereignty carve-outs. “Compute freeport” is the generic policy category; actual places should have grounded names such as Model Freeport, Bonded Cloud Zone, Sovereign Cloud Concession, Data Entrepôt, or Compute Concession. Residents receive jobs and stability but live inside compute rationing and behavior scores.
Biosecure Health Zones
Biotech and hospital operators run pathogen-controlled districts, organ farms, gene clinics, fertility services, and body-subscription infrastructure. Safety and bodily control are inseparable.
Critical Minerals Protectorates
Mining firms, security contractors, export-credit agencies, and host ministries administer mineral basins. Roads, clinics, and wages come with extraction, tailings, surveillance, and insurgency.
Port, Cable, and Logistics Corridors
Terminal operators, customs platforms, telecom consortia, and private police control trade arteries. These places decide what arrives, what leaves, whose feed is clean, and whose money clears.
Climate Migration Work-Towns
Employers provide visas, dorms, clinics, food, remittance rails, and cooling. Losing work can mean losing residency, medicine, and family access.
Global Blocs and Map Logics
These are not final faction names. They are world-map pressures that can later produce factions, alliances, campaign regions, and conflicts.
North Atlantic Climate Compact
A law-insurance-finance-compute civilization built around climate liability, certified feeds, Arctic access, offshore wind, nuclear/hydro power, and regulation.
Heroic face: preserves due process, archives, climate courts, and public accountability.
Horrific face: exports actuarial exclusion, debt receivership, sensor mandates, and polite abandonment.
White Sky stance: controlled maintenance, strict liability, fear of termination shock, anxiety over North Atlantic circulation changes.
Visual identity: pale sky over glass floodgates, polished court towers, insurer seals, public dashboards, memorials to saved districts and abandoned ones.
Pacific Compute-Manufacturing Mesh
A chain of fabs, cable hubs, ports, robotics centers, battery plants, and trusted hardware zones.
Heroic face: technical competence, manufacturing depth, resilient logistics, disciplined reconstruction.
Horrific face: labor discipline, supply-chain caste, water sacrifice, and zero-tolerance security.
White Sky stance: divided; it protects coasts but threatens monsoons, solar yield, and fab-water stability.
Visual identity: cleanrooms, sea walls, cable bunkers, drone ports, neon against white daytime haze.
Equatorial Grievance Belt
A broad set of harmed, exploited, resource-rich, youthful, and politically divergent regions across wet tropics, mineral belts, rainforests, islands, and heat-exposed cities.
Heroic face: climate justice, resource sovereignty, demographic vitality, anti-extraction politics, new cultures of adaptation.
Horrific face: concession elites, armed resource politics, bio-extraction, hostage migration corridors, and factional fragmentation.
White Sky stance: often hostile; accuses sky operators of solar theft, monsoon theft, and climate occupation.
Visual identity: humid glare, storm walls, copper/cobalt roads, solar protests, body-clinic queues, blue-paint slogans.
Desert Desalination and Solar States
High-control states and corporate cities that manufacture habitability through desalination, cooling, sovereign wealth, helium/LNG, solar, ports, and migrant labor.
Heroic face: engineering mastery, managed survival, high-tech refuge, water production.
Horrific face: labor dependence, heat apartheid, citizenship tiers, sealed luxury under lethal skies.
White Sky stance: resents dimming and may demand compensation or local tuning authority.
Visual identity: mirrored shade canopies, desalination cathedrals, night markets, sealed transit, white-sky glare on solar fields.
Arctic-Subarctic Frontier
A dangerous northern frontier of shipping, cables, minerals, cold datacenters, fisheries, launch/sensor stations, military patrols, and indigenous sovereignty.
Heroic face: new autonomy movements, cold refuge, hard survival, sensor science, route rescue.
Horrific face: extraction rush, militarized insurance, displaced communities, private navies, black-ice disasters.
White Sky stance: ambivalent; cooling protects some systems while limiting access and extraction.
Visual identity: white sky merging with snow haze, black water, drone buoys, icebreaker convoys, undersea cable shrines.
Continental Granaries and Nutrient States
Food, fertilizer, seed IP, water timing, autonomous agriculture, fermentation protein, and sewage nutrient recovery become strategic power.
Heroic face: feeds people, preserves soil, protects local agriculture.
Horrific face: calorie diplomacy, seed DRM, nutrient surveillance, export coercion.
White Sky stance: practical; supports whichever sky regime stabilizes yields.
Visual identity: pale crop fields, autonomous harvesters, nutrient police, grain-port fortresses, mycoprotein vats.
Free-Net and Exclusion Commons
A non-state layer of abandoned, uninsurable, insurgent, mesh-networked, floating, underground, and disaster-scarred territories.
Heroic face: refuge, archive, mutual aid, black-market medicine, anti-corporate truth work.
Horrific face: scams, cults, malware, gang rule, bad body hacks, false memories, poisoned feeds.
White Sky stance: remembers what official systems erase, but not cleanly.
Visual identity: illegal antennas, scavenged solar skins, broken flood walls, community cooling shrines, graffiti maps, dead-mall vats, Free-Net reliquaries.
Wars That Fit This World
Corridor Wars
Conflicts over ports, rail spines, cable landings, repair fleets, dam roads, desalination pipelines, launch corridors, and HVDC routes.
They are limited enough for corporate/state actors to deny escalation, but strategically decisive.
Maintenance Wars
Conflicts over White Sky infrastructure, cooling grids, pumps, filters, sensor basins, and climate-model custody.
The objective is rarely conquest. It is to control whose life-support remains credible.
Actuarial Wars
Conflicts fought through insurance withdrawal, credit downgrades, disaster-model leaks, risk-score sabotage, and parametric payout manipulation.
A city can be destroyed financially before a missile lands.
Body Rights Wars
Conflicts over whether leased bodies, prosthetics, gene packages, reproductive services, immune systems, and organ support can be repossessed, downgraded, inherited, hacked, or nationalized.
Champions can emerge as symbols of bodily sovereignty.
Provenance Wars
Conflicts over which feed records are believed: casualty counts, weather data, atrocity footage, land titles, election results, migration claims, and Echo continuity.
Reality itself becomes a supply chain.
Nutrient and Calorie Wars
Conflicts over fertilizer, grain routes, seed DRM, synthetic-protein vats, fishing grounds, and urban nutrient recovery.
These wars feel less glamorous than chip wars but may decide mass legitimacy.
Role of Champions in This Map
Champions should be more than super-units. They are people whose bodies, reputations, Echoes, or battlefield actions can puncture layered sovereignty.
A Champion can be:

a walking legal crisis whose body violates ownership categories;
a celebrity whose presence stabilizes a sacrificed territory;
a factional saint of Blue Restoration, Sky Loyalty, body sovereignty, Free-Net truth, or corporate salvation;
a deniable corporate asset leased across jurisdictions;
a local warlord who controls a cooling corridor;
a person whose Echo proves or destabilizes a disputed past;
a symbol strong enough to override actuarial classifications and platform bans.

The world needs Champions because ordinary institutions have become too layered, deniable, and technical for people to believe in. Champions are visible proof that history still has faces.
Visual / Sensory Identity

A permanent pale sky, bright enough to feel exposed and false.
Neon and holograms in daytime, not just night, because the world needs color against white glare.
Blue as luxury, nostalgia, contraband, therapy, or rebellion.
Seawalls, pump towers, heat shelters, cooling stacks, drone buoys, cable bunkers, and body clinics as everyday landmarks.
Rich territories are over-maintained: polished filters, verified feeds, smooth transit, climate dashboards, quiet private security.
Poor territories are over-measured: risk warnings, debt screens, cheap sensors, unreliable apps, emergency sirens, broken shade nets.
Corporate borders marked by service quality: the air changes, the feed cleans up, the drones become quieter, the water tastes different.
Sacrificed zones are not empty wastelands. They are dense with improvisation, cults, repairs, archives, bad medicine, and desperate beauty.

In-World Beliefs

Sky Loyalists: the White Sky is ugly life support; opposing it is mass murder.
Blue Restorationists: the White Sky is corporate occupation of the atmosphere.
Albedo Sovereignists: no distant actor should tune another region’s weather.
Corporate Humanists: private life-support saved civilization where states failed.
Receivership Realists: democracy without pumps, power, and clinics is theatre.
Free-Net Archivists: official climate truth is curated liability management.
Body Sovereigns: survival modifications must become rights, not subscriptions.
Nutrient Nationalists: food, waste, seed, and soil are the real sovereignty.
Arctic Openers: cooling robbed the north of its future access.
Heat Justice movements: habitable hours are a human right.

Open Questions

Should the default campaign map show national borders first, or maintenance/sacrifice/contest zones first?
Which bloc is strongest in the starting year?
Which region benefited most from White Sky and therefore defends it sincerely?
Which region was most visibly harmed by White Sky and therefore supplies the strongest opposition?
Are corporate regions normalized everywhere, or concentrated in former/debt-distressed developmental economies plus disaster-hit rich cities?
Should one corporation be the first White Sky mover, or should its identity remain hidden behind a rescue consortium?
Do players mostly command factions inside one region, or move across the global corporate archipelago?

cultures/champion-worship.title: Champion Worship
cultures/champion-worship.content:
Champion Worship
One-Line Summary
Champion worship is the social, parasocial, religious, political, and celebrity-like fixation on Champions as stronger, truer, or more historically important people in a rapidly changing world.
What It Is
Many people in Neon Champions do not merely admire Champions. They orient themselves around them.
A Champion may become:

celebrity
protector
revolutionary icon
corporate mascot
saint
warlord
sex symbol
prophet of transhuman evolution
proof that strong leaders exist
proof that ordinary people are obsolete
living brand
object of hate

Why It Matters
The world is changing too quickly for ordinary institutions to feel stable. Bodies, identities, jobs, cities, memories, and political borders are all unstable.
In that instability, Champions offer a seductive idea: history still has protagonists. Some people are not merely adapted to the new world; they are meant to rule it, survive it, or define it.
In the AI age, this becomes even sharper. Champions are often worshipped as proof that humans still possess something virtual intelligence cannot own: embodied courage, charismatic risk, moral drama, sacrifice, presence, and the ability to become a living symbol. This can be sincere, comforting, manipulative, or all three.
Ideological Charge
Champion worship can carry a transhumanist and Nietzschean/übermensch-like myth. Different factions interpret this differently:

liberation: Champions prove humanity can exceed imposed limits
domination: Champions prove inequality is natural and leadership belongs to the strong
salvation: Champions protect ordinary people from chaos
resentment: Champions are manufactured idols used to pacify the masses
horror: Champions are the first visible signs of humanity being replaced
human exceptionalism: Champions prove that AI can assist, imitate, and predict, but cannot fully take over what makes humans historically meaningful
anti-AI reassurance: Champions are sold as living evidence that the AI restraint compact is preserving something real

Chorus Exchange
Chorus Exchange industrializes Champion worship. It hosts Patron Channels, saint clips, rankings, sponsorship markets, donation swarms, bounty boards, scandal containment, and posthumous Echo features.
A Champion’s fame can become a strategic resource because Chorus turns parasocial attachment into liquidity, recruitment, morale, consumer behavior, and sometimes violence.
Parasocial Dynamics
People may believe they know Champions through:

combat feeds
sponsorship streams
faction propaganda
martyr stories
scandal archives
illegal bodycam recordings
arena mythologies
stylized battle reports
Net simulations and personality echoes

A fan may know a Champion’s diet, scars, kill-count, preferred weapons, lovers, slogans, and rumored mutations while knowing nothing true about the person.
Dangers
Champion worship can produce:

authoritarian politics
faction recruitment pipelines
copycat body modification
anti-Champion terrorism
cults of martyrdom
celebrity assassinations
black-market relic trade
willingness to excuse atrocities
ordinary people surrendering agency to supposed strong leaders

Open Questions

Are there official Champion leagues, rankings, or licenses?
Do factions manufacture parasocial relationships deliberately?
Are there anti-Champion movements?
Can a Champion’s fame itself become a strategic resource?
What happens when a beloved Champion is revealed to be fake, manufactured, dead, copied, or controlled?
Did Champion worship begin as a response to AI anxiety before being captured by corporations, factions, cults, militaries, and other entities?
What happens when a Champion’s charisma, judgment, or symbolic aura is revealed to have been VI-assisted or manufactured by prediction systems?

design-bridges/greenland-faction-unit-ro.content:
Greenland Faction Unit Rosters
One-Line Summary
The first-campaign factions still make sense if their units are not generic soldiers in different colors, but expressions of what each faction believes survival should become: local sovereignty, proprietary climate maintenance, certified polar control, treaty peacekeeping, atmospheric commons, concession logistics, or weaponized biosecurity.
Faction Fit Verdict
Yes, the current faction set still makes sense. The strongest playable core is:

Home Rule Coalition — local legitimacy, terrain knowledge, rescue, community defense, consent politics. As of 2026-06-18, this is a soft-canon/provisional game-facing faction name for EPIC-008 planning, not hard canon.
QXZ Meridian Arctic Mandate — White Sky maintenance, climate liability, proprietary rescue, elite infrastructure security.
Barents Research Group / Polar Certification Combine — polar data, route certification, sensors, drones, “neutral” scientific control.
Digital Peacekeeping Directorate / the Blue / the Blues — Treaty Net, public infrastructure, cyber peacekeeping, mandate-limited force.

The best antagonist/side-faction layer is:

Open Sky / Blue Week Cells — atmospheric commons, leaks, sabotage, direct action, risky truth.
Janus-Kestrel Mining-Logistics Consortium — ports, cargo identity, extraction finance, private security, concession contracts.
Tundra Biosecurity / Wildlife Control Program — better as neutral dwelling chain or subfaction first; full faction later if the animal-control fantasy proves strong.

Cultural Naming Note
Avoid using Kalaallit as a faction brand. It is the real endonym connected to Greenlandic national and cultural identity, and using it as a playable strategy-faction label risks turning a living people into game IP.
Safer current placeholder: Home Rule Coalition. As of 2026-06-18 it is approved as a soft-canon/provisional game-facing faction name for EPIC-008 planning. It describes a political formation in the fiction without claiming to represent all Greenlandic people or appropriating the endonym as a brand. Real Greenland / Kalaallit Nunaat can still be treated respectfully as a place with local sovereignty, municipalities, languages, communities, and interests. See home-rule-coalition.
Shared Unit Design Rules

Units are “creatures” in HoMM terms, but diegetically they are squads, drone groups, specialist teams, animals, platform swarms, or contracted crews.
Avoid pure soldier reskins. Every unit line should imply a source building, social class, legal status, and upgrade path.
Tactical battles should allow ranged fire, cover, terrain, hacking, morale/publicity effects, extraction objectives, and Intel preservation.
Upgrades should look like better doctrine, better equipment, stronger legal mandate, cleaner feed access, or more exploitative contracts — not fantasy evolution.
Elite units should be ethically or politically expensive, not just stronger.

Roster Scale Proposal
For MVP, each playable faction needs only:

3 recruitable unit lines;
1 Champion;
1 neutral/shared recruit line;
1 signature tactical mechanic.

For vertical slice, expand each faction to:

6-7 unit lines, HoMM-style;
basic and upgraded variants;
one faction-specific recruitment site;
one elite or controversial unit.

Home Rule Coalition
Fantasy
Local sovereignty under pressure. The faction wins by knowing the land, protecting communities, controlling legitimacy, and making outsiders pay for every shortcut.
Visual Identity
Weathered civic gear, sealift containers, municipal rescue orange, hunter/fisher equipment, patched drones, sled/ATV logistics, community mesh radios, snow camouflage, old Danish/Greenlandic/UN markings repainted by local councils.
Tactical Identity
Defensive mobility, terrain bonuses, rescue/sustain, ambushes, legitimacy/proof generation, lower raw tech but better Arctic adaptation.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Settlement WatchCouncil GuardDefensive infantryLocal militia, good in settlements/outposts, weak in open elite fights.2Sled Logistics TeamWhiteout CouriersSupport/mobilityImproves movement, extraction, supply, can evacuate wounded or Intel.3Hunter-ScoutsFjord StalkersRecon/skirmisherTerrain stealth, marks targets, strong in snow/fjord maps.4SAR Drone CrewRescue Mesh WingSupport dronesHeals/stabilizes, reveals terrain, can recover proof from battlefield.5Fishery HardhatsHarbor Defense UnionTough melee/riot lineIndustrial workers with exosuits/tools; strong near ports/factories.6Compact NegotiatorsConsent WardensSoft-control/supportBuffs allies, debuffs corporate units, generates Proof/Legitimacy on objectives.7Heritage Ranger TeamCivic VanguardElite adaptive squadHigh morale, terrain mastery, anti-drone tools; politically costly if lost.
Signature Mechanic
Consent Network — controlling civic sites gives defensive buffs and Proof. Destroying local infrastructure weakens this faction but damages the attacker’s legitimacy.
Strongest Unit Ideas

Fjord Stalkers: scouts who can disappear in bad weather and mark enemy units for ambush.
Consent Wardens: not fantasy priests; lawyers, elders, translators, feed witnesses, and negotiators who turn legitimacy into tactical effects.
Civic Vanguard: elite local defenders, not super-soldiers; their power is competence, local trust, and terrain.

QXZ Meridian Arctic Mandate
Fantasy
Proprietary life support. QXZ believes climate stability is too fragile for democratic improvisation and that White Sky infrastructure must be protected even when people hate it.
Visual Identity
White/pearl corporate armor, pale-blue hazard lights, clean sealed suits, atmospheric maintenance logos, stratospheric sensor drones, climate-service vehicles, sterile clinics, liability seals, mirrored visors reflecting a white sky.
Tactical Identity
High-tech combined arms, hazard control, shields/barriers, climate-station buffs, expensive elite units, strong defensive infrastructure, weak local legitimacy.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Meridian SecurityMandate Response TeamInfantryClean corporate security, disciplined, costly.2Aerosol TechsSkyline EngineersSupport/repairRepairs drones/structures, deploys cover, stabilizes climate hazards.3Liability MedicsContinuity CliniciansHeal/cleanseMedical support with insurance/protocol flavor; may “stabilize” enemies for capture.4Strato Sensor SwarmMeridian Eye SwarmRecon/droneReveals stealth, marks targets, improves ranged accuracy.5Climate BulwarkAlbedo BastionHeavy defenderShield unit, area denial, protects infrastructure.6Termination-Risk TeamEmergency Suppression UnitControl/anti-sabotageLocks down zones, counters Open Sky/Free-Net actions.7White Sky CustodiansMeridian PaladinsEliteIconic corporate knight analogue; terrifying because they really may be preventing catastrophe.
Signature Mechanic
Stability Protocols — QXZ can reduce environmental hazards and protect infrastructure, but some actions increase Public Distrust or local resistance.
Strongest Unit Ideas

Albedo Bastion: a mobile shield/maintenance platform — the “tower unit” that fits tactical battles.
Termination-Risk Team: emergency force justified by catastrophe modeling; tactically strong, politically ugly.
Meridian Paladins: not literal paladins; elite climate-infrastructure guardians with almost religious PR framing.

Barents Research Group / Polar Certification Combine
Fantasy
Whoever certifies the Arctic owns the Arctic. Barents does not need to conquer territory openly; it controls maps, risk scores, route permissions, sensor truth, and rescue data.
Visual Identity
Research orange, oceanic teal, black sensor fabric, expedition frames, autonomous buoys, ice radar, lab coats under armor, branded “safety” tags, neutral scientific typography that hides corporate teeth.
Tactical Identity
Scouting, targeting, route control, drones, debuffs through sensor superiority, strong map knowledge, medium combat durability.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Field SurveyorsCertified Route TeamScout/supportFinds hidden paths and hazards; weak combat.2Ice Radar OperatorsCryo-Mapping CellReveal/debuffExposes stealth, reduces enemy mobility.3Research DronesBoreal Sensor NetDrone swarmCheap recon/harass; enables precision attacks.4Rescue ContractorsDenied-Zone RespondersMobile infantrySAR with private-security edge.5Cable DiversUnder-Ice SaboteursSpecialistCoastal/under-ice maps; disables Net/energy nodes.6Risk ActuariesCertification BoardCommand/supportRewrites tactical risk: buffs allies, debuffs enemies, manipulates initiative.7Polar Exclusion TeamBlack-Ice WardensElite control squadArea denial, sensor dominance, anti-stealth/anti-drone.
Signature Mechanic
Certified Route — Barents can mark safe/unsafe routes. In battle, it can designate zones as “certified” for ally bonuses or “excluded” for enemy penalties.
Strongest Unit Ideas

Risk Actuaries: ridiculous name on purpose, but cyberpunk-strong — people whose models decide who is allowed to move.
Cable Divers: great Greenland-specific unit; ports, cables, under-ice infrastructure, sabotage.
Black-Ice Wardens: elite polar cyber-security / physical exclusion team; name also nods to cyberpunk ICE.

Digital Peacekeeping Directorate — the Blue / the Blues
Fantasy
Peacekeeping in a networked world where public access, hospital routing, evidence chains, and AGI quarantine are battlefields. The Blues are necessary, distrusted, mandate-bound, and always late until suddenly they are everywhere.
Visual Identity
UN blue helmets translated into AR/cyber gear: blue bands, blue-lane overlays, white vehicles, humanitarian markings, hard legal labels, transparent shields, court-admissible bodycams, portable relay masts.
Tactical Identity
Defensive control, nonlethal options, anti-hack, proof stabilization, emergency routing, strong objective play, limited aggression unless mandate conditions are met.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Blue Line OperatorsTreaty Net GuardsBasic infantry/securityProtects nodes, modest combat, strong near civic infrastructure.2Civic Relay TechsBlue-Lane EngineersSupportDeploys relays, restores comms, repairs Net objectives.3Mandate ObserversEvidentiary OfficersProof/supportRecords actions, protects evidence, punishes unlawful attacks.4Cyber PeacekeepersQuarantine Breach TeamAnti-hack specialistCounters Digital-Net actions and rogue systems.5Humanitarian ConvoyProtected Relief ColumnSustain/objectiveHeals, supplies, shields civilians; slow but hard to ignore.6Blue Shield SquadDirectorate Intervention UnitControl infantryRiot/nonlethal tools, shields, zone control.7AGI Compact WardensBlue Mandate ExecutorsEliteAnti-rogue-model / quarantine unit; legally terrifying when unleashed.
Signature Mechanic
Mandate Threshold — some powerful Blue actions unlock only after treaty violations, civilian danger, Net collapse, or AGI-quarantine risk is documented.
Strongest Unit Ideas

Evidentiary Officers: they make battlefield actions legally real; very Neon Champions.
Protected Relief Column: a “caravan” unit that is tactically awkward but strategically valuable.
Blue Mandate Executors: elite force that feels scary because it arrives with legal inevitability.

Open Sky / Blue Week Cells
Fantasy
The sky belongs to everyone, or no one survives with dignity. Open Sky is part activist network, part leak collective, part sabotage ecology, part desperate public conscience.
Visual Identity
Patchwork cold-weather clothes, anti-corporate blue-sky symbols, pirate AR paint, cheap drones, repurposed climbing gear, solar scraps, printed masks, hand-painted slogans over hacked corporate equipment.
Tactical Identity
Ambush, sabotage, mobility, morale shocks, leaks, fragile units with high disruption potential, strong against infrastructure and public narrative.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Protest LineDirect Action BlocCheap infantry/controlWeak damage, can block/occupy objectives.2Free-Net RunnersPirate Relay GhostsHacker/scoutMoves through Net layer, reveals hidden proof.3Banner DronesSky Graffiti SwarmMorale/mediaDebuffs enemy legitimacy, spreads visibility.4Climber-SaboteursMeridian CuttersInfrastructure damageStrong vs stations, relays, vehicles.5Leak LawyersCommons AdvocatesSupport/controlTurns captured Intel/Proof into public penalties.6Weather Hack CellBlue Break CellRisky specialCan trigger environmental chaos; may backfire.7Unceiling VanguardOpen Sky MartyrsElite irregularHigh disruption, morale effect, politically explosive casualties.
Signature Mechanic
Make It Public — Open Sky can turn battlefield events into Proof/Legitimacy swings. The more visible the fight, the more dangerous they become.
Pushback
Open Sky should not be the default “good rebels.” Some cells are reckless. Some are infiltrated. Some cause real harm. Their moral force comes from being partly right and tactically dangerous.
Janus-Kestrel Mining-Logistics Consortium
Fantasy
Development as capture. Janus-Kestrel wins by making every port, road, cargo tag, payroll, and mineral claim pass through its systems.
Visual Identity
Industrial yellow/black, port authority marks, container geometry, cargo drones, private security matte armor, mining exosuits, finance-contract UI, customs seals, logistics barcodes.
Tactical Identity
Build tempo, armored workers, private security, logistics buffs, resource extraction, contract penalties, strong economy but vulnerable to legitimacy attacks.
Unit Lines





























































TierBasic UnitUpgraded UnitRoleNotes1Site SecurityConcession GuardsInfantryCheap private guards tied to claims.2Cargo HandlersBonded Logistics CrewSupportImproves movement/supply; can fortify objectives.3Prospecting TeamsClaim EngineersEconomy/scoutMarks resource sites; weak combat.4Mining ExosuitsHeavy Extraction FramesHeavy melee/utilityDurable, can damage terrain/cover.5Customs BrokersContract EnforcersControl/supportSlows enemy movement, taxes routes, manipulates objectives.6Port DronesKestrel Cargo SwarmRanged/droneMobile ranged pressure; stronger near supply lines.7Concession BreakersJanus Black Ledger UnitElitePrivate military/accounting hybrid; punishes enemies economically and tactically.
Signature Mechanic
Concession Contract — Janus-Kestrel can mark sites as concession zones, gaining resource advantages and imposing movement/tax penalties, but increasing local resistance and Open Sky/local hostility.
Tundra Biosecurity / Wildlife Control Program
Recommended Role
Start as a neutral dwelling chain, scenario hazard, or subfaction. It is cool, but making it a full faction too early risks tonal silliness unless grounded hard.
Fantasy
Wildlife management turned into command infrastructure. The horror is not animal magic; it is telemetry, stress ecology, disease monitoring, drones, collars, and bioacoustic coercion turning animals into a contested security layer.
Unit / Dwelling Ideas








































SiteRecruit / EffectRoleWildlife Patrol StationSled Dog Logistics TeamMovement/rescue supportBioacoustic TowerMusk Ox Stampede RigArea denial / disruptionRaven Tagging LabRaven Sensor SwarmScouting / signal spoofingPolar Bear Collar FacilityPolar Bear Bio-Tag AlphaRare elite beast / ethical scandalCoastal Buoy NurserySeal/Narwhal Buoy NetworkCoastal detection / route controlQuarantine BlindParasite Panic EventScenario hazard, not normal recruit
Pushback
Use polar bears sparingly. They should be rare, frightening, and reputationally radioactive — not a standard cavalry unit.
Neutral / Shared Units
These can appear as dwellings, mercenary sites, map rewards, or local recruitment:


















































UnitRoleGood ForArctic Freelancersflexible infantrycommon neutral guard/recruitSmuggler-SAR Crewmobile supportmedicine, evacuation, dark routesBlack Clinic Medicsrisky healing/body modsbiotech eventsFree-Net Cellhacker/supportIntel and map revealWeather Station Staffobjective supportWhite Sky / hazard missionsPort Militiadefensive infantryports/fish plantsDrone Salvagerseconomy/reconwrecks, caches, IntelEcho Witnessmorale/proof anomalyrare story unit, use carefully
Tactical Battle Feel
A Neon Champions tactical battle should not look like two modern armies lining up. It should look like a contested site:

fish plant loading yard;
radar dome service road;
ice runway;
hydro intake tunnel;
server bunker;
port container stack;
White Sky calibration mast;
evacuated settlement street;
under-ice cable landing.

Objects matter:

server racks can be captured for Intel;
relay masts can change Net visibility;
civilians/proof witnesses can constrain attacks;
climate equipment can create hazards;
drones can be hacked instead of destroyed;
extracting a VIP may matter more than wiping enemies.

MVP Recommendation
For the first tactical prototype, use two factions and six units total:
Home Rule Coalition

Settlement Watch / Council Guard
Hunter-Scouts / Fjord Stalkers
SAR Drone Crew / Rescue Mesh Wing

QXZ Meridian

Meridian Security / Mandate Response Team
Aerosol Techs / Skyline Engineers
Climate Bulwark / Albedo Bastion

Scenario: contested White Sky sensor station near a fishery/airstrip. Optional Intel objective: capture the server rack before QXZ wipes it or before local systems collapse.
Open Questions

Should unit tiers mirror HoMM exactly, or use fewer broader tactical roles?
Are upgraded variants permanent building unlocks, Intel upgrades, or both?
Do Champions command stacks like HoMM, squads on a grid, or hybrid formations?
Should nonlethal capture be a general mechanic or mostly a Blue/Kalaallit feature?
How many units can fit tactically before combat becomes too slow?

factions/factions-as-evolutionary-philos.title: Factions as Evolutionary Philosophies
factions/factions-as-evolutionary-philos.content:
Factions as Evolutionary Philosophies
One-Line Summary
Neon Champions factions should not be mere color palettes or combat rosters; each should express a rival philosophy of what humanity should become under White Sky, compute scarcity, biotech dependency, polluted reality, and Champion myth.
Core Rule
Every major faction should answer the same question differently:
What is the legitimate next form of human life?
Possible answers include owned enhancement, liberated mutation, human exceptionalism, machine emergence, climate adaptation, body sovereignty, corporate citizenship, local survival, memory continuity, or restoration of the old sky.
Shared Pressures
Factions form around world pressures already in the vault:

White Sky and climate inequality;
compute and energy sovereignty;
body modification as subscription;
polluted feeds and targeted accounting;
Digital-Net access and contamination;
Champion ownership, worship, and legitimacy;
Echoes and post-death identity.

Candidate Faction Axes
These are not final factions yet. They are axes to prevent shallow faction design.
Body Ownership vs Body Sovereignty
Some factions believe bodies are platforms maintained by institutions. Others believe no person is free while their organs, upgrades, or climate adaptations can be throttled.
Human Exceptionalism vs Machine Emergence
Some factions treat Champions as proof that humans remain history’s protagonists. Others see the AI restraint compact as cowardice and want machine minds, VI liberation, or Digital-Net evolution.
White Sky Defense vs Blue Restoration
Some factions see the White Sky as civilizational mercy. Others see it as climate occupation, corporate ceiling, or planetary wound.
Managed Reality vs Free Net
Some factions defend filtered, stabilized feeds as necessary social medicine. Others want raw data, cracked archives, and dangerous truth even if it destabilizes society.
Adaptation vs Restoration
Some factions embrace engineered bodies and climate-zone identities. Others want old ecologies, old bodies, old skies, or old legal categories back.
Design Pressure
For every future faction, define:

its evolutionary answer;
what it considers human;
who owns bodies;
how it treats Champions;
how it treats VI and compute scarcity;
its position on the White Sky;
its relationship to the Digital-Net;
its heroic version;
its horrific version;
its internal contradiction.

Game-Relevance Notes
This page is a design constraint for later faction pages. It should push every faction toward a distinct worldview, economy, body practice, unit identity, Champion logic, territory style, and campaign conflict.
Open Questions

How many playable factions should exist initially?
Should factions be corporations, city-states, ideologies, cultures, platforms, military blocs, or hybrids?
Which faction is most sympathetic but dangerous?
Which faction looks monstrous but has the strongest moral argument?

Start Here

Canon: World Rules

agi-compact-and-compute-deterrence — reviewed soft-canon world rule: AGI/ASI are prohibited by compact because they create compute-MAD and incumbent-obsolescence risks; the compact stabilizes great powers while pushing violence into proxy conflict.

virtual-intelligence-and-compute-scarcity — seed world rule: ubiquitous generative AI and corporate VI exist, but confirmed AGI is absent or hidden; compute and energy scarcity shape politics.
white-sky — seed world rule: corporate-initiated planetary albedo intervention that cooled Earth through a maintained reflective sky while turning climate survival into unequal, proprietary infrastructure.
world-map-and-political-economy — seed world rule: the post-White-Sky world as maintained, sacrificed, and contested territories layered over states, corporations, climate infrastructure, and resource corridors.

Canon: History / Timeline

Cultures

Characters
Technologies

Species / Beings
Organizations

barents-research-group — reviewed soft-canon Arctic/polar megacorp: an innocent-sounding research and maritime-safety corporation whose data, route certification, extraction concessions, cables, and rescue/security arms make it a polar power.

Conflicts
Mysteries

Glossary
